Whole cashew-nut feeding in dyslipidemic rats (Dias 2023, PMID:37597587) and purified cashew anacardic acids in Swiss mice (Gomes Junior 2018, PMID:29573147, linked to processed kernels via Mattison 2018) both show anxiolytic-like easing without any controlled worsening evidence. Absence of human clinical anxiety RCTs, non-PD rodent assays, abstract-only reporting in Dias 2023, and non-kernel leaf/pomace separation (Srichomphu 2022) keep the easing lean at minimal_signal.

No human clinical study, observational Parkinson's cohort, or controlled animal experiment tests roasted cashew nuts on apathy severity. Available human cashew trials (Meneguelli 2024, n=68; Baer 2019, n=42) report cardiometabolic endpoints only (outcome_fit=unusable) and traditional ethnobotanical records supply no clinical apathy severity evidence, leaving the claim open.

No isolated human trial evaluates roasted cashew nuts on attention impairment. Nijssen 2023 (PMID:37296019, n=28) bundled cashews with three other tree nuts (attribution_fit=remote) and found no change in CANTAB executive function or psychomotor speed, Theodore 2021 (PMID:33330927) confirmed no isolated cashew cognitive trials, and rodent maze tests assess spatial memory rather than attention impairment (outcome_fit=remote), keeping the claim open.

One controlled rotenone rat PD experiment (Medeiros-Linard 2018, PMID:29520721) showed oral anacardic acids (>=10 mg/kg/d) prevented rotenone-induced open-field locomotor slowing (outcome_fit=partial), supported by nigrostriatal TH protection (Augusto 2020) and quantified anacardic acids in processed cashew kernels (Mattison 2018). Isolated constituent dosing, non-roasted matrix, and absence of human PD UPDRS-III bradykinesia trials limit inference to minimal_signal.

Controlled human cashew nut studies measure intestinal permeability (Meneguelli 2024, PMC11431763, n=64, null between groups), acute beverage GI symptoms (Santana 2026, n=27, null), and fecal energy digestibility (Baer 2018, n=18) without scoring constipation severity or Bristol stool form (outcome_fit=remote/unusable), while mouse colitis (Siracusa 2020) and non-nut bark/leaf antidiarrheal studies do not evaluate constipation, leaving the claim open.

No human Parkinson's trial assesses roasted cashew nuts on daily OFF time or levodopa motor fluctuations. Rico 2016 (PMC4779481) documents cashew kernel protein content (21.3 g/100 g) without levodopa interaction testing, and rotenone anacardic-acid studies (Medeiros-Linard 2018, Augusto 2020) lack fluctuation endpoints (outcome_fit=remote), keeping the claim open.

Extract/constituent matrices and absence of human depression or PD studies limit the tier to minimal_signal.

Evidence remains open for dried cherry reducing anxiety severity in Parkinson disease. Four randomized double-blind tart-cherry concentrate/juice trials outside PD found no statistically significant anxiety or calmness benefit: Sinclair et al. 2022 (PMID:35564709, n=44; tart cherry null on STAI state/trait vs placebo and worse than blueberry on trait anxiety p=0.038), Losso et al. 2018 (PMID:28901958, n=8; STAI null), Kimble et al. 2022 (PMID:35109960, n=49; Bond-Lader Calm p=0.699), and Keane et al. 2016 (PMID:27989253, n=27; acute mood null). Only one small crossover of a formulated freeze-dried sweet-cherry plus maltodextrin/ascorbic-acid drink (Garrido et al. 2012, n=30 across 3 age strata) reported subgroup STAI improvements in middle-aged/elderly healthy adults without overall pooled estimates, leaving neither direction defensible for whole dried cherry in PD.

Two independent human randomized trials of tart or sweet cherry products report statistically significant improvements on validated attention/concentration subtests outside Parkinson disease: Kimble et al. 2022 (PMID:35109960, PMC9723490, n=50 middle-aged adults, 12-week DB-RCT of Montmorency tart cherry concentrate) improved Digit Vigilance sustained-attention accuracy by +3.3% (95% CI 0.2 to 6.4%, p=0.035) and reduced false alarms by -1.2 (95% CI -2.0 to -0.4, p=0.005), though RVIP was null (p=0.194); Arbizu et al. 2025 (PMID:40077655, n=40 obese adults, 30-day single-blind RCT of dark sweet cherry drink plus 3 g cherry powder) improved Digit Span Forward concentration (p=0.006) and Backward (p=0.01), though TMT and DSST sustained attention were null. Supporting context includes Chai et al. 2019 (PMID:31287117, n=37 older adults; within-group visual sustained attention p<0.0001). Competing null trials include acute concentrate (Keane 2016, n=27) and pediatric ADHD (Soltanifar 2023, n=70, p=0.317; 28.6% abdominal pain, 31.4% asthenia). Because no trial tests whole dried cherries or diagnosed Parkinson attention impairment, the surviving signal is restricted to minimal_signal (eases).

No human clinical trial tests dried cherry on bradykinesia severity in Parkinson disease. Chai et al. 2019 (PMID:31287117, n=37 cognitively normal older adults) reported faster computerized movement time (-10.4, p=0.03) after 12 weeks of Montmorency tart cherry juice, a non-PD screen-touch psychomotor metric distinct from MDS-UPDRS bradykinesia; Filaferro et al. 2022 (PMID:35204092, PMC8868341) improved locomotor climbing in rotenone-exposed Drosophila using sweet cherry anthocyanin extract, an invertebrate extract proxy that does not establish clinical human bradykinesia effects.

No controlled clinical trial tests raw whole cherries on constipation severity in Parkinson disease or chronic constipation. Sinclair et al. 2025 (PMID:40003718, n=35 mild-to-moderate ulcerative colitis) found Montmorency tart cherry juice improved IBDQ and Simple Clinical Colitis Activity Index (reflecting colitis diarrhea/urgency, not constipation), while Arbizu et al. 2024 (PMID:39228354, n=40) reported fecal microbiota shifts without constipation outcomes and Hillman & Chrismas 2021 (PMID:34604282, n=58) found null gut microbiome effects. Safety notes include sporadic diarrhea or abdominal pain in tart cherry concentrate trials (Shenouda 2022, Soltanifar 2023).

No human Parkinson disease clinical trial, observational study, or pharmacokinetic interaction study evaluates dried cherry on levodopa motor fluctuations or daily OFF time. Only a preclinical rotenone Drosophila extract study (Filaferro 2022, PMID:35204092) and general non-PD cherry trials exist, supplying no OFF-time contrast.

Two double-blind randomized controlled trials of Montmorency tart cherry juice/concentrate that directly administered the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS) found NO statistically significant improvement vs placebo: Sinclair et al. 2022 (PMID:35564709, n=44) and Losso et al. 2018 (PMID:28901958, n=8 older adults with insomnia). Although Kimble et al. 2022 (PMID:35109960, n=48) reported higher Bond-Lader alertness during cognitive testing (+5.9%, p=0.013) with tart cherry concentrate, acute task alertness is distinct from clinical daytime sleepiness, and a multi-ingredient blend (Langan-Evans 2023, PMID:36094342) cannot isolate cherry. One Parkinson UK forum member (2018) with daytime dozing tried cherry juice alongside mirtazapine briefly before stopping. With both ESS trials null and no raw-cherry PD trial, the claim remains open.

Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trials measuring validated depression scales with tart cherry products found NO benefit over placebo: Sinclair et al. 2022 (PMID:35564709, n=44; Beck Depression Inventory null for tart cherry concentrate vs placebo, whereas blueberry improved BDI p=0.041), Losso et al. 2018 (PMID:28901958, n=8; BDI-II null), and Kimble et al. 2022 (PMID:35109960, n=48; Bond-Lader Content null p=0.166). Garrido et al. 2012 evaluated non-clinical VAS mood/fitness items in healthy adults without a depression severity scale. No trial tests whole dried cherries or Parkinson depression.

No clinical trial tests dried cherry or tart cherry products on REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) or dream enactment frequency in Parkinson disease. While tart cherry contains trace melatonin and improved general insomnia sleep duration in small non-PD crossover trials (Losso 2018, Howatson 2012), Tucker et al. 2024 (PMID:39683518, n=34) found 500 mg/day tart cherry powder capsules had no effect on objective REM sleep duration (p>0.05) and no study measured dream-enactment episodes. A 2026 Parkinson UK forum discussion on melatonin for vivid dreams/dream enactment included a secondhand suggestion to eat 1/2 cup tart cherries before bed without any reported patient outcome.

No human clinical trial, observational study, or experiential Parkinson account evaluates dried cherry on sialorrhea or drooling severity. Tart/sweet cherry trials in older adults and clinical cohorts (Kimble 2022, Sinclair 2022, Shenouda 2022) report no drooling adverse events or salivary-flow comparisons.

No human Parkinson disease trial, levodopa-interaction study, or mammalian AIMs experiment tests raw cherry on levodopa-induced dyskinesia severity. Preclinical sweet-cherry anthocyanin extract research (Filaferro 2022, PMID:35204092) examined rotenone-exposed Drosophila climbing without modeling dyskinesia.

Two independent human randomized controlled trials using anthocyanin-rich sweet cherry (Prunus avium) juice/powder outside Parkinson disease report statistically significant improvements on executive-related subtests, with zero trials showing worsening: Kent et al. 2017 (PMID:26482148, n=49 older adults >=70 y with mild-to-moderate dementia, 12-week RCT of 200 mL/day sweet cherry juice) significantly improved verbal fluency (executive/lexical retrieval, p=0.014) alongside short-term (p=0.014) and long-term memory (p<=0.001); Arbizu et al. 2025 (PMID:40077655, n=40 obese adults, 30-day single-blind RCT of dark sweet cherry drink + powder) significantly improved Digit Span Backward working-memory manipulation (p=0.01), though Trail Making Test (TMT) and DSST showed no between-group difference. Competing null executive/working-memory trials include Kimble et al. 2022 (PMID:35109960, n=40; 3-back accuracy p=0.608, RT p=0.930), Chai et al. 2019 (PMID:31287117, n=37; spatial working memory borderline within-group p=0.06), and Keane et al. 2016 (PMID:27989253, n=27 acute null). Because evidence derives from cherry juice/powder outside PD and several executive subtests (3-back, TMT) were null, the lean against worsening is strictly minimal_signal (eases).

No human clinical trial or observational study evaluates raw cherry intake on fall frequency in Parkinson disease or older adults. Although Losso et al. 2018 (PMID:28901958) noted in background that hypnotic drugs raise fall risk in older adults with insomnia as a rationale for studying tart cherry juice, neither Losso 2018 nor any other cherry trial measured fall incidence.

No human Parkinson disease clinical trial, observational study, or animal experiment assesses raw cherry on freezing of gait (FOG) frequency. Rotenone Drosophila locomotor assays (Filaferro 2022) and non-PD knee OA walking time (Schumacher 2013) do not model or measure freezing of gait.

No human clinical trial tests dried cherry on fine hand dexterity (e.g., Nine-Hole Peg Test, Purdue Pegboard, or MDS-UPDRS finger tapping) in Parkinson disease. Hooper et al. 2021 (PMID:34126996, n=13 resistance-trained men) reported preserved post-squat maximal handgrip dynamometer strength (+1.7 kg vs -2.0 kg placebo at 24 h, p=0.017) with 500 mg/day tart cherry extract capsules, but maximal isometric grip force after heavy barbell squats is distinct from fine finger dexterity impairment and enrolled healthy athletes rather than PD patients.

Five independent double-blind randomized placebo-controlled crossover or parallel trials outside Parkinson disease report sleep improvements with tart cherry (Prunus cerasus) or freeze-dried sweet cherry (Prunus avium) products, and zero trials report worsening: Pigeon et al. 2010 (PMID:20438325, n=15 older adults with chronic insomnia; lower ISI insomnia severity and WASO vs placebo), Losso et al. 2018 (PMID:28901958, n=8 insomnia completers; +84 min PSG sleep time p=0.0182, PSQI sleep efficiency p=0.03), Howatson et al. 2012 (PMID:22038497, n=20; higher actigraphy sleep time/efficiency and urinary melatonin p<0.05), Garrido et al. 2013 (PMID:23732552, PMC12878997, n=30; reconstituted freeze-dried Jerte Valley sweet cherry improved actigraphy sleep efficiency, latency, and awakenings), and Chung et al. 2022 (PMID:36011907, n=19 athletes; actigraphy WASO p=0.044, TTB p=0.015). CRITICAL COMPETING NULL EVIDENCE: Tucker et al. 2024 (PMID:39683518, n=34 overweight/obese adults with sleep complaints) found 500 mg/day powdered Montmorency tart cherry capsules had NO effect on any objective sleep metric or ISI/PSQI (all p>0.05), and three healthy-adult trials (Hillman 2026 PMID:35790450 n=44, Kimble 2022 PMC9723490 n=50, Sinclair 2022 PMID:35564709 n=44) were likewise null. Parkinson UK forum accounts document temporary perceived help from cherry juice alongside practical high-volume adherence barriers (2018) and tart-cherry melatonin suggestions (2026). Together, the clinical-insomnia older-adult RCTs and healthy actigraphy trials support a minimal_signal against worsening (eases), strictly capped at 50.005 due to the 2024 null powder-capsule trial, null healthy-sleeper trials, liquid/powder vs whole-dried-fruit preparation gap, and lack of a Parkinson insomnia RCT.
No human clinical trial, observational cohort, or Parkinson community report evaluates raw cherry on hypophonia or voice loudness (dB SPL, VHI, MDS-UPDRS speech volume).

No human clinical trial tests raw cherries on Parkinson extrapyramidal muscle rigidity (MDS-UPDRS item 3.3). Sports-recovery trials of tart cherry juice/powder measured post-exercise range of motion (ROM) and relaxed elbow angle after eccentric muscle damage—not Parkinson cogwheel/lead-pipe rigidity—and found null ROM/elbow-angle contrasts (Connolly 2006 p=0.85, Squires 2024 p>0.3, Lamb 2019 p>0.05, Daab 2026 meta-analysis null).

No human clinical trial, cohort study, or animal experiment tests dietary raw cherries on hyposmia or olfactory impairment severity in Parkinson disease. Cherry aroma appears strictly as a scratch-and-sniff stimulus item in UPSIT odor-identification tests rather than an oral dietary intervention.

No human clinical trial tests raw cherries on orthostatic hypotension or standing lightheadedness in Parkinson disease. Three systematic reviews and meta-analyses of resting blood pressure RCTs—Norouzzadeh et al. 2023 (PMID:37809623, 21 RCTs), Moosavian et al. 2022 (PMID:36038032, 10 RCTs), and Eslami et al. 2022 (PMID:35108661, 7 RCTs n=201)—found neutral pooled effects on resting SBP and DBP (p>0.05), alongside null chronic BP RCTs (Kimble 2021 PMC8145763 n=50, Sinclair 2022 n=44, Hillman 2026 n=44). Individual trials reporting acute or modest resting SBP lowering (Keane 2016, Kent 2017, Chai 2018, Arbizu 2023) measured supine/seated BP rather than orthostatic drop, and systemic BP reduction would not ease orthostatic hypotension.

Multiple independent human double-blind RCTs and a large gout case-crossover study outside Parkinson disease demonstrate statistically significant pain/flare easing from tart or fresh cherry products, with zero trials showing pain worsening: Shenouda et al. 2022 (PMID:34275765, n=48 analyzed breast-cancer aromatase-inhibitor arthralgia, 6-week DB-RCT) reduced VAS joint pain by 34.7% vs 1.4% placebo (p=0.034; 2 diarrhea withdrawals); Kuehl et al. 2010 (PMID:20459662, n=54 runners DB-RCT) reduced post-race VAS muscle pain increase (12+/-18 mm vs 37+/-20 mm placebo, p<0.001); Connolly et al. 2006 (PMID:16790484, n=14 crossover DB-RCT) reduced eccentric arm pain (p=0.017); Zhang et al. 2012 (PMID:23023818, n=633 gout case-crossover) linked 2-day fresh cherry intake to 35% lower gout flare odds (OR 0.65, 95% CI 0.50-0.85; extract OR 0.55); and Xu et al. 2026 network meta-analysis (PMID:42666369, 30 trials n=595) found tart cherry reduced 24h, 48h, and 72h DOMS vs placebo (low certainty). CRITICAL COMPETING NULL TRIALS: Schumacher et al. 2013 (PMID:23727631, n=58 knee OA crossover) found no significant between-treatment WOMAC difference vs placebo (p=0.16 despite within-arm p<0.01); Elliot et al. 2010 (n=14 fibromyalgia) was non-significant (VAS p=0.10); powdered tart cherry trials Hagele et al. 2026 (PMID:41683264, n=40, soreness VAS p=0.838) and Squires et al. 2024 (PMID:39203845, n=22, VAS p>0.3) were null; Stamp et al. 2020 (PMID:31891407, n=50 gout 28d) found null gout flare frequency (p=0.76); Lamb 2019 (n=36), Abbott 2020 (n=10), Morehen 2021 (n=11), Gao 2024 (n=12), and Daab 2026 athlete meta-analysis (19 trials) were null on soreness. Evidence remains open for cooked chickpeas worsening anxiety severity in Parkinson disease. Human chickpea amino-acid digestibility data (Kashyap 2024 PMID:39307282, tryptophan digestibility 72.6%) provide biochemical context only without mood testing.

Evidence remains open for canned chickpeas affecting apathy severity in Parkinson disease. Comprehensive Oracle catalog, live PubMed, and ClinicalTrials.gov searches found zero human clinical trials, observational PD cohorts, or animal models testing cooked, canned, or roasted chickpeas on this symptom. Existing human chickpea feeding interventions (such as Dahl et al. 2014 PMID:26067078, n=12 GI tolerance; Mussie et al. 2026 PMID:41947250 amaranth-chickpea flatbread cluster RCT) measured gastrointestinal or anthropometric outcomes without assessing Parkinson neuropsychiatric, bulbar, sensory, or facial-motor symptoms, and traditional Persian/Ayurvedic records (CULT:2019-Persian-Ayurvedic-Chickpea-Traditions) provide general culinary-restorative heritage only.

Evidence remains open for roasted chickpeas affecting attention impairment in Parkinson disease. In Scott et al. 2017 (PMID:28832514, PMC5622679, n=40 completed adults >=50 years), 1 cup/day chickpeas was pooled optionally with 1 medium potato as the low-lutein control arm versus fresh avocado over 6 months, with no significant Group x Time interaction on any CANTAB cognitive test (including RVIP sustained attention and Stockings of Cambridge executive planning; sustained attention improved from baseline in avocado only, while PAL practice improved in both arms). In aged mice, Kadyan et al. 2024 (PMID:38352704, PMC10864001) directly tested 5% chickpea-derived resistant starch and observed null performance on T-maze working memory and novel object recognition/location (only lentil and pinto bean resistant starches improved T-maze). MiniMeal (PMC13631491, 2026) is an unpublished protocol combining oat bran and chickpeas. No controlled human study isolates roasted chickpeas on Parkinson attention or executive dysfunction.

Evidence remains open for cooked chickpeas affecting bradykinesia severity in Parkinson disease. No human clinical trial tests cooked, canned, or roasted chickpeas on Parkinson motor endpoints. The only preclinical behavioral study directly testing a whole-chickpea dietary carbohydrate fraction in aged mice—Kadyan et al. 2024 (PMID:38352704, 5% chickpea resistant starch)—found null effects on grip strength, rotarod coordination, hanging-wire endurance, and open-field mobility. While multiple rodent PD toxin models (Wang 2015 PMID:26394281; Yu 2017 PMID:29217997; El-Sherbeeny 2020 PMID:32977283; Li 2021 PMID:31050314; Tian 2026 PMID:41483847) report dopaminergic neuroprotection and motor sparing with purified isoflavone biochanin A (10-60 mg/kg), biochanin A is a purified pharmaceutical constituent occurring across red clover, soy, and chickpeas rather than a culinary preparation of whole chickpeas; macaque feeding confirmed Cicer arietinum lacks neurolathyric motor toxicity (Hugon 1988 PMID:3347349). Because purified biochanin A cannot establish whole-food efficacy and whole-chickpea resistant starch motor testing was null, the evidence stays open.

Two human dietary crossover interventions outside Parkinson disease reported improved perceived bowel health or bowel function with canned drained chickpeas: Murty, Pittaway & Ball 2010 (PMID:19945492; companion cohort to Pittaway 2008 PMID:18502235, n=42 completed Australian adults, 12-week ordered crossover of ~104 g/day canned drained chickpeas vs 4-week habitual diet) reported improved perceived frequency of defecation, ease of defecation, and softer stool consistency; Pittaway et al. 2007 (PMID:17906185, n=27 free-living adults, 5-week randomized crossover of canned drained chickpeas plus 30% chickpea-flour baked foods vs fiber-matched wheat) reported significantly better perceived general bowel health. A competing smaller randomized crossover in healthy non-constipated adults (Dahl et al. 2014 PMID:26067078, same n=12 cohort as Fernando et al. 2010 PMID:21831757; 200 g/day canned chickpeas x 3 weeks) found no change in daily stool frequency (1.7 vs 1.5/day) alongside mild flatulence (p<0.001) and mild bloating (p<0.001). Public Parkinson community discussion (HealthUnlocked 2024) notes mixed experience with bean/chickpea meals helping bowel regularity for one contributor while others required osmotic laxatives. Because human studies sampled healthy non-constipated adults using subjective bowel-health endpoints with one null small crossover and no diagnosed Parkinson constipation RCT, the surviving easing lean is restricted to minimal_signal (eases).

Evidence remains open for canned chickpeas reducing daily OFF time in Parkinson disease, consistent with prior Round 2 legume evaluations (black beans, adzuki beans, black-eyed peas). No clinical trial has tested canned chickpeas on Parkinson levodopa pharmacokinetics or daily OFF time. Mechanistic human protein-digestibility and kinetic studies show that cooked chickpea protein has lower true ileal indispensable amino acid digestibility (~74.6%, Kashyap 2019 PMID:31374575) and tryptophan digestibility (72.6%, Kashyap 2024 PMID:39307282) than animal proteins (~90-96%), intact chickpea cell walls attenuate postprandial serum amino acid appearance (Perez-Moral 2023 PMID:36257266), and a 40 g wheat-chickpea blend produced lower postprandial plasma leucine and EAA spikes than chicken (Kouw 2022 PMID:34881688, n=24, p<0.001). However, chickpeas still supply dietary large neutral amino acids, an unverified UV-vis claim of L-DOPA in sprouted chickpeas (Gouigah 2016 in local HAL follow-up) does not establish clinically active L-DOPA in canned chickpeas, and public Parkinson forum reports (Parkinson's UK 2011 and 2013-2025 threads) show heterogeneous personal tolerance where modest lunchtime hummus is often used during protein redistribution yet wearing-off can still persist.

Existing human chickpea feeding interventions (such as Dahl et al. 2014 PMID:26067078, n=12 GI tolerance; Mussie et al. 2026 PMID:41947250 amaranth-chickpea flatbread cluster RCT) measured gastrointestinal or anthropometric outcomes without assessing Parkinson neuropsychiatric, bulbar, sensory, or facial-motor symptoms, and traditional Persian/Ayurvedic records (CULT:2019-Persian-Ayurvedic-Chickpea-Traditions) provide general culinary-restorative heritage only.

Evidence remains open for cooked chickpeas affecting muscle rigidity severity in Parkinson disease. No human clinical trial tests cooked, canned, or roasted chickpeas on Parkinson motor endpoints. The only preclinical behavioral study directly testing a whole-chickpea dietary carbohydrate fraction in aged mice—Kadyan et al. 2024 (PMID:38352704, 5% chickpea resistant starch)—found null effects on grip strength, rotarod coordination, hanging-wire endurance, and open-field mobility. While multiple rodent PD toxin models (Wang 2015 PMID:26394281; Yu 2017 PMID:29217997; El-Sherbeeny 2020 PMID:32977283; Li 2021 PMID:31050314; Tian 2026 PMID:41483847) report dopaminergic neuroprotection and motor sparing with purified isoflavone biochanin A (10-60 mg/kg), biochanin A is a purified pharmaceutical constituent occurring across red clover, soy, and chickpeas rather than a culinary preparation of whole chickpeas; macaque feeding confirmed Cicer arietinum lacks neurolathyric motor toxicity (Hugon 1988 PMID:3347349). Because purified biochanin A cannot establish whole-food efficacy and whole-chickpea resistant starch motor testing was null, the evidence stays open.

Evidence remains open for roasted chickpeas worsening orthostatic lightheadedness severity in Parkinson disease. Because no trial isolates roasted chickpeas or tests orthostatic standing hypotension or postprandial lightheadedness in PD, neither worsening nor easing is established.

Evidence remains open for cooked chickpeas worsening pain severity in Parkinson disease. Minimal directional lean toward easing bradykinesia (Maybe True, 50.005): Gunhyuk Park's 2014 dissertation directly tested oral fresh Coriandrum sativum aerial-part extract in MPTP PD mice on timed pole turning (111.99% vs 153.10%) and pole descent (102.58% vs 178.44%), reinforced by the same Kyung Hee / Oh research program's 2026 oral leaf-extract study in MPTP and Proteus mirabilis PD mouse models (PMID:40972938, grip strength 2.65-2.75 N vs 2.31 N plus pole/rotarod rescue) and independent 6-OHDA rat nigral TH rescue with heated coriander leaf extract (Saeki 2022, PMID:35922685). Coriander seed/fruit MPTP data (Koppula 2021) are excluded as a distinct plant part; non-human animal models, extract versus raw culinary leaf, and shared-program overlap cap confidence at minimal_signal.

No human or controlled animal study tests isolated fresh cilantro leaves for constipation or bowel frequency. Available human bowel trials either tested multi-herb laxative mixtures dominated by senna and aloe using coriander fruit/seed (Ghafarzadegan 2025, PMID:39951927), three-herb Carmint drops (Vejdani 2006, PMID:16868824), or a two-herb Bunium persicum plus C. sativum dyspepsia formula (Azimi 2024, PMID:38981452). Lee 2026 (PMID:40972938) observed colonic inflammation and alpha-synuclein rescue in gut-first PD mice without reporting stool frequency or constipation endpoints.

No human Parkinson's trial, pharmacokinetic levodopa-absorption study, or dietary cohort evaluates fresh cilantro leaves against daily OFF time. Preclinical leaf-extract PD mouse studies (Lee 2026, PMID:40972938; Park 2014) did not model levodopa motor fluctuations, and culinary leafy-herb servings supply negligible dietary protein (<0.1 g per garnish) relative to levodopa-competing large neutral amino acid loads.

No clinical or preclinical study tests dried cilantro leaves for daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale or wakefulness). The sole aerial-part sleep study (Rakhshandeh 2012, PMID:21988208) found parenteral hydroalcoholic extract prolonged barbiturate-induced sedation in mice—an anesthetic sleep-potentiation assay that neither tests oral dried leaves nor measures daytime alertness—while Alqudah 2024 tested coriander seeds.

No human clinical trial or isolated controlled animal depression study tests fresh cilantro leaves on depressive symptoms. Alqudah 2024 (NCT05999071) reported lower HADS depression scores using powdered coriander SEEDS in non-PD university students and is strictly excluded on plant-part grounds (leaf aldehydes vs seed linalool). Puthallath 2020 examined cilantro leaf fractions only on mouse anxiety mazes without depression assays.

No polysomnography, REM-sleep behavior disorder (RBD), or patient-reported dream enactment study exists for dried cilantro leaves. Mouse aerial-part pentobarbital sleep prolongation (Rakhshandeh 2012, PMID:21988208) and neuronal KCNQ2/3 potassium-channel activation by leaf (E)-2-dodecenal (Manville & Abbott 2019, PMID:31311306) provide no REM-atonia or dream-enactment evidence.

No human clinical trial or levodopa-induced dyskinesia (LID) animal experiment tests dried cilantro leaves. Published cilantro leaf PD studies (Lee 2026, PMID:40972938; Saeki 2022, PMID:35922685) modeled nigrostriatal toxin injury without chronic levodopa priming or abnormal involuntary movement (AIM) dyskinesia scoring.

No human or animal study tests dried cilantro leaves for Parkinson's dystonia or focal muscle spasms. Neuronal KCNQ2/3 potassium-channel activation by cilantro leaf (E)-2-dodecenal (Manville & Abbott 2019, PMID:31311306) and aerial-part PTZ seizure attenuation (Karami 2015, PMID:26056549) address epileptic excitability rather than extrapyramidal dystonia.

Mani et al. 2011 (PMID:20848667) directly fed fresh Coriandrum sativum leaves (5%, 10%, 15% w/w in mouse diet x 45 days) and observed reversal of aging-, scopolamine-, and diazepam-induced associative/spatial memory deficits on elevated plus maze transfer latency and passive avoidance alongside brain AChE inhibition. However, rodent spatial/avoidance memory tasks do not measure prefrontal executive function (outcome_fit=remote), no human cilantro-leaf cognitive trial exists (Alqudah 2024 used coriander seeds), and thus fresh cilantro effects on Parkinson's executive function remain open.

No human prospective fall-frequency trial or cohort evaluates dried cilantro leaves. Rodent motor-coordination assays (Park 2014 fresh aerial-part extract; Lee 2026 leaf extract, PMID:40972938; Rodrigues 2019 freeze-dried leaf/stalk extract in MeHg-exposed rat offspring, PMID:31408720) measure laboratory rotarod or beam performance rather than human clinical fall rates.

No human clinical trial or controlled animal anti-fatigue study tests fresh cilantro leaves on fatigue severity. Published leaf PD studies (Lee 2026, PMID:40972938) measured muscle grip strength and motor coordination rather than subjective or exertional fatigue, and community discussions document culinary garnish use only.

No human Parkinson's trial or gait-freezing assessment evaluates fresh cilantro leaves. Preclinical fresh aerial-part and leaf extract studies in MPTP mice (Park 2014; Lee 2026, PMID:40972938) measure pole descent and rotarod performance rather than episodic freezing of gait.

No human clinical study evaluates dried cilantro leaves on fine hand dexterity (pegboard, finger-tapping, or MDS-UPDRS hand tasks). Preclinical leaf studies (Lee 2026, PMID:40972938) measured gross murine grip strength and pole descent rather than fine manual dexterity.

No human sleep or insomnia trial tests dried cilantro leaves (Alqudah 2024, NCT05999071, tested powdered coriander SEEDS and is excluded on strict leaf-versus-seed separation). The sole aerial-part sleep study (Rakhshandeh 2012, PMID:21988208) injected dried aerial-part hydroalcoholic extract and solvent fractions intraperitoneally into healthy mice and observed prolonged pentobarbital sleeping time—a single parenteral barbiturate-potentiation animal assay that cannot establish oral culinary dried-leaf effects on human Parkinson's insomnia.

No clinical, acoustic, or preclinical study evaluates fresh cilantro leaves on vocal loudness or Parkinson's hypophonia. Traditional and community sources document culinary seasoning use without vocal-intensity outcomes.

No human trial or passive-joint-resistance rigidity assay tests dried cilantro leaves. Coriander leaf PD animal models (Lee 2026, PMID:40972938; Saeki 2022, PMID:35922685) assessed grip strength, rotarod/pole behavior, and nigral dopamine preservation rather than muscle tone or cogwheel rigidity.

No human olfactory-rehabilitation or Parkinson's hyposmia trial tests dried cilantro leaves. Structural biology (Wang et al. 2026, Cell, PMID:41570822) decoded reversible covalent binding of cilantro leaf aldehydes to human olfactory receptor OR6A2—explaining genetic 'soapy' taste/smell aversion—and a 2018 Parkinson's UK forum discussion recommended non-chili spices including coriander for meal enjoyment during taste changes, neither of which tests whether eating dried cilantro restores olfactory function.

Strict leaf-versus-seed separation excludes Delavar Kasmaei 2016 (PMID:26889386), which tested coriander FRUIT/SEED syrup in migraine rather than cilantro leaves. Among leaf studies, Jiao 2021 (PMID:33550058, leaf AuNP analgesia) was formally RETRACTED in 2026 (PMID:42527244) and is excluded, leaving only Begnami 2018 (PMID:29864950), where an intraperitoneal ethyl-acetate fraction of dried leaves and stems reduced mouse nociception while concurrently depressing open-field locomotion at 100-300 mg/kg (sedation confound). A single parenteral solvent-fraction mouse study with locomotor depression and zero human leaf pain trials leaves dried cilantro pain effects open.

Minimal directional lean toward easing postural instability (Maybe False, 50.005, opposing the frozen 'worsens' claim): oral fresh coriander aerial-part extract rescued MPTP PD mouse rotarod balance retention (84.84% vs 29.68% of control in Park 2014), corroborated within the same Kyung Hee research program by Lee 2026 (PMID:40972938, rotarod/motor improvement in MPTP and Proteus mirabilis PD mice, individual rotarod tables paywalled) and independently by Rodrigues 2019 (PMID:31408720, freeze-dried cilantro leaf/stalk extract reducing balance-beam foot slips in methylmercury-exposed rat offspring) plus Puthallath 2020 showing zero rotarod impairment in healthy mice. Coriander seed MPTP rotarod data (Koppula 2021) are excluded as a distinct plant part; animal-only evidence and extract versus raw leaf cap confidence at minimal_signal.

No human Parkinson's trial or tremor-specific animal assay evaluates fresh cilantro leaves on resting tremor. Preclinical leaf PD models (Park 2014; Lee 2026, PMID:40972938; Saeki 2022, PMID:35922685) assessed pole descent, rotarod, grip force, and nigral dopamine preservation without quantifying tremor.

No human gait-kinematics study or murine footprint stride-length assay tests dried cilantro leaves. Published leaf PD models (Lee 2026, PMID:40972938; Park 2014) reported grip strength, pole test, and rotarod rather than step/stride length, aligning with Round 1 0679 (dried cilantro walking slowness open).

No clinical micrographia or handwriting kinematics study tests fresh cilantro leaves in Parkinson's disease. Animal leaf-extract models (Lee 2026, PMID:40972938) cannot capture human handwriting amplitude.
No human speech-pathology, listener-intelligibility, or dysarthria study evaluates fresh cilantro leaves in Parkinson's disease.

No human urology or overactive-bladder trial tests dried cilantro leaves. Thuraisingam 2019 observed that oral water and methanol extracts of powdered shade-dried cilantro leaves increased 6-hour urine volume (diuresis) in healthy rats—a diuretic fluid-output assay that does not test detrusor overactivity or urgency relief (and diuresis would not indicate urgency reduction).

No human clinical trial, pharmacovigilance series, or Parkinson's psychosis cohort evaluates dried cilantro leaves on visual hallucinations. Leaf aldehyde KCNQ2/3 studies (Manville & Abbott 2019, PMID:31311306) and mouse memory studies (Mani 2011, PMID:20848667) do not model visual hallucinations.

Direct human oral ground-cinnamon testing (Lee et al. 2014, PMID:25516316, n=48 older adults >=60 y with pre-diabetes, DB-RCT) found 2 g oral cinnamon at breakfast produced NO change in post-prandial working memory/attention versus placebo (null, whereas turmeric improved it). Nakhaee et al. 2024 (PMID:36652384) confirmed only two human cinnamon cognition studies overall (null oral Lee 2014 and non-oral chewing-gum/aroma). Chao 2025 (PMID:40908892) tested inhaled 6-odor olfactory training (non-oral bundle), and Rangasamy 2026 (PMID:42221706, corrected republication of retracted 2021 paper) tested isolated sodium benzoate in TBI mice. Neither harm nor benefit for oral ground cinnamon on Parkinson's attention is established.

Minimal directional lean toward easing bradykinesia (Maybe True, 50.005), tightly calibrated with Round 1 0889 (ground cinnamon walking slowness): four independent animal PD programs demonstrate consistent oral motor/pole-test bradykinesia rescue with zero opposing trials—(1) Rush/Pahan oral ground Ceylon Cinnamomum verum powder in A53T transgenic mice (Raha 2021, PMID:32889602, timed pole turn/descent improved; 2025 correction PMID:40072646 affected separate Fig 6 NaB panels) and MPTP mice (Khasnavis & Pahan 2014, PMID:24946862; Patel 2019, PMID:31119595); (2) independent Jiao/Wu oral cinnamaldehyde program in MPTP mice (Jiao 2024, PMC11688134, n=72 pole climbing; Wu 2022, PMID:36604895) and reserpine PD rats (Jiao 2024, PMID:38621979); (3) independent Xu 2020 oral A-type cinnamon procyanidin oligomers in MPTP mice (PMID:32386222); and (4) Buyukakilli 2026 rotenone PD rat neuromuscular improvement (PMID:42210599). Capped at minimal_signal by absence of human PD RCTs, while flagging hepatotoxic coumarin differences between Cassia and Ceylon cinnamon (Abraham 2011, PMID:21462332).

No human Parkinson's trial or levodopa fluctuation diary tests isolated ground cinnamon for daily OFF time. Phillips et al. 2018 (PMID:30098269) included cinnamon in both low-fat and ketogenic diet menus with no cinnamon intake contrast, and Sauerbier et al. 2018 (PMC6312592) did not isolate ground cinnamon versus OFF hours.

Minimal directional lean toward easing depressive symptoms (Maybe False, 50.005, directly opposing the frozen 'worsens' claim): six independent controlled rodent depression studies across oral Cinnamomum verum bark extract (Yusha'u 2023, PMID:38696678 OSFST; Kim 2021, PMID:34425473 LPS FST/TST), oral cinnamon essential oil (Ma 2023, PMID:37416658 CUMS sucrose preference/FST/TST; Sohrabi 2017, PMID:28868126 FST/TST), and oral cinnamaldehyde (Yao 2015, PMID:25556926 middle-aged rat CUMS; Zhou 2025, PMID:41160920 IFN-alpha mice) consistently show antidepressant-like easing with zero studies reporting mood worsening. Zhang 2026 (PMID:42892342, n=328 brain tumor RCT) reported HADS depression easing with INHALED cinnamon LEAF oil (excluded from direct oral bark scoring on route and plant part), and Sauerbier 2018 (PMC6312592) found no cross-sectional HADS mood link in PD. Non-human oral models and absence of an isolated human oral ground-cinnamon depression RCT cap confidence at minimal_signal.

Lee et al. 2014 (PMID:25516316, n=48 older adults >=60 y, DB-RCT) directly tested 2 g oral ground cinnamon at breakfast and found NO significant change in working memory versus placebo (null), and Nakhaee 2024 (PMID:36652384) verified no other isolated oral cinnamon executive-function RCT exists. Inhaled 6-odor olfactory training (Chao 2025, PMID:40908892) cannot isolate oral ground cinnamon. Evidence for Parkinson's executive function remains open.

No clinical fall-frequency trial or prospective cohort evaluates oral ground cinnamon in Parkinson's disease. Rodent PD rotarod balance studies (Raha 2021, PMID:32889602; Jiao 2024, PMC11688134) do not directly count human clinical falls, and a 2018 caregiver report noted continued unsteadiness requiring a walking stick despite daily Ceylon cinnamon.

No human trial or observational PD gait study evaluates ground cinnamon for freezing of gait. Preclinical A53T and MPTP mouse cinnamon models (Raha 2021, PMID:32889602; Patel 2019, PMID:31119595) test open-field and pole locomotion rather than episodic freezing of gait.

No clinical pegboard, finger-tapping, or MDS-UPDRS hand-dexterity trial tests ground cinnamon in Parkinson's disease. Rodent PD studies (Raha 2021, PMID:32889602; Jiao 2024, PMC11688134) test gross locomotion and pole climbing rather than human fine manual dexterity.

No isolated oral ground-cinnamon sleep or insomnia RCT exists in Parkinson's disease or general adults. Both human cinnamon sleep studies used non-oral routes: Zhang et al. 2026 (PMID:42892342, n=328 brain tumor patients) tested INHALED cinnamon LEAF oil aromatherapy (wrong route and wrong plant part), and Steels et al. 2019 (PMID:31780001) tested an INTRANASAL cinnamon bark extract spray for allergic rhinitis (sleep sub-score secondary to nasal relief). Therefore oral ground-cinnamon insomnia effects remain open.

Minimal directional lean toward easing postural instability (Maybe True, 50.005): three independent preclinical PD research programs consistently show oral ground Ceylon cinnamon or its key bark constituents rescue rotarod balance/postural coordination with zero opposing trials—(1) Rush/Pahan oral ground Ceylon Cinnamomum verum powder in A53T transgenic mice (Raha 2021, PMID:32889602, rotarod latency rescued; 2025 correction PMID:40072646 affected separate Fig 6 NaB panels) and MPTP mice (Khasnavis & Pahan 2014, PMID:24946862; Patel 2019, PMID:31119595); (2) independent Jiao/Wu oral cinnamaldehyde MPTP mice (Jiao 2024, PMC11688134, n=72; Wu 2022, PMID:36604895) and reserpine PD rats (Jiao 2024, PMID:38621979); and (3) independent Xu 2020 oral A-type cinnamon procyanidin oligomers in MPTP mice (PMID:32386222). Tempered by absence of human PD clinical balance trials and a real-world caregiver observation of ongoing unsteadiness despite daily Ceylon cinnamon (2018 PUK thread).

No human clinical trial or isolated tremor assay tests ground cinnamon for Parkinson's rest tremor. Preclinical MPTP and A53T mouse cinnamon studies (Raha 2021, PMID:32889602; Khasnavis 2014, PMID:24946862; Jiao 2024, PMID:38621979) evaluated pole climbing, rotarod, and open-field movement rather than clinical rest tremor, and Persian traditional medicine references cite cinnamon inside multi-herb tremor formulas without isolated clinical evidence.

No human gait-kinematics trial measures stride length after oral ground cinnamon. Although Rush oral ground Ceylon cinnamon mouse studies (Raha 2021, PMID:32889602; Khasnavis 2014, PMID:24946862) showed improved open-field movement speed and distance (anchoring Round 1 0889 walking slowness), they did not directly isolate human or footprint stride length, and a 2018 caregiver report noted persistent small-step shuffling despite daily Ceylon cinnamon.

No human dysphagia or videofluoroscopic swallowing trial tests culinary ground cinnamon in Parkinson's disease. While inhaling dry loose cinnamon powder is a well-known choking/aspiration hazard (and concentrated cassia poses coumarin liver-safety concerns, Abraham 2011, PMID:21462332), no clinical study quantifies whether culinary food-incorporated ground cinnamon worsens Parkinson's dysphagia.

No placebo-controlled human clinical trial tests oral ground clove for attention in Parkinson's disease or general adults. Bell et al. 2021 (n=52 completers, PD excluded, sponsor-funded) compared two active doses of clove-derived beta-caryophyllene plus rice-bran oil without a placebo arm, printed inconsistent arm counts (29 vs 26 per arm), and measured self-reported Cognitive Failures Questionnaire totals rather than objective attention tasks. Mohan 2019 (PMID:31064377, Clovinol n=13) measured only blood glucose. Evidence remains open.

No human clinical trial tests oral ground clove for constipation (studies of 'clover' are botanically unrelated). The sole relevant animal motility experiment (Agbaje 2008, PMID:19062476) showed oral hot aqueous Syzygium aromaticum extract (300-700 mg/kg) accelerated charcoal propulsion in healthy normal mice via an atropine-sensitive cholinergic mechanism and contracted isolated rabbit ileum—a single healthy-animal transit assay without constipation modeling or human confirmation—keeping constipation effects in Parkinson's disease open.

Minimal directional lean toward easing depressive symptoms (Maybe True, 50.005): three independent oral Syzygium aromaticum studies align toward easing with zero opposing depression reports—(1) Sadeh et al. 2020 randomized 60 non-PD depressed adults to oral oil-reduced clove bud extract capsules plus citalopram vs placebo plus citalopram and reported lower week-6 Beck Depression Inventory scores (7.0 vs 10.9, p=0.009; explicitly capped at reliability_fit=remote due to Table 2 misprinted as 'anxiety', unverified IRCT20190309042979N1, and conflicting vol 13/14 publication dates); (2) Liu et al. 2015 (PMID:25590367) demonstrated oral clove essential oil reversed mouse FST, TST, and CUMS sucrose-preference anhedonia while restoring hippocampal pERK/pCREB/BDNF; and (3) Brahmi et al. 2025 (PMID:39795390, PMC11723110) showed oral clove essential oil reduced FST immobility in ochratoxin-A-exposed rats. Serious reporting flaws in Sadeh 2020, adjunct citalopram, extract/essential-oil preparations vs culinary ground clove, and non-PD populations cap confidence strictly at minimal_signal.

No human polysomnography, REM-sleep behavior disorder (RBD), or dream-enactment study tests oral ground clove. Komori et al. 2006 (PMID:16857858) tested inhaled clove oil on rat pentobarbital sleep (null) without EEG REM-atonia measurements.

No human Parkinson's dyskinesia trial exists for ground clove, and preclinical eugenol/clove PD studies exhibit a critical timing-dependent divergence: whereas pre-lesion eugenol attenuated 6-OHDA or MPTP neurotoxicity (Kabuto 2007, PMID:17329831; Moreira Vasconcelos 2020, PMID:32353201; Vora 2022 pretreatment, PMID:36002316), POST-lesion oral eugenol WORSENED striatal dopamine depletion (Kabuto & Yamanushi 2011, PMID:21769642) and WORSENED MPTP akinesia/motor deficits (Vora 2022 post-treatment). Moreira Vasconcelos 2020 combined eugenol with levodopa on rotational behavior without establishing clinical dyskinesia relief. Because post-lesion animal harm directly opposes pre-lesion neuroprotection and zero human PD dyskinesia data exist, dyskinesia remains open with a clear timing-safety caution.

No human Parkinson's dystonia study tests ground clove, and preclinical eugenol PD models show divergent pre- versus post-lesion dopaminergic outcomes (Kabuto 2007 vs Kabuto & Yamanushi 2011; Vora 2022) without evaluating dystonia. Concentrated clove oil ingestion was associated in one case report with transient fasciculations, dysarthria, and dysphagia (AlBaazi & Hassoun 2022), not culinary ground clove dystonia.

Full-text verification of Alembagheri et al. 2023 (PMID:38444713, PMC10912872, 28-day rat weight-loaded forced swimming test) confirmed that oral aqueous clove extract (333 mg/kg/d) produced NO statistically significant change in swimming endurance, blood glucose, LDH, or TNF-alpha versus control (null, whereas myrtle berries and apple increased swimming time). Hawkins et al. 2022 (PMID:35341944) tested an INHALED 4-oil aromatherapy blend (thyme, orange, clove bud, frankincense) in post-COVID women (non-oral route and bundled oils), and Mammen et al. 2018 (PMID:30234415, n=16 crossover) showed oral Clovinol polyphenols lowered composite acute alcohol-hangover scores (-55.34%), not PD fatigue. Thus oral ground clove effects on Parkinson's fatigue remain open.

No human trial tests oral ground clove on fine hand dexterity in Parkinson's disease. Preclinical eugenol PD rodent models (Kabuto & Yamanushi 2011; Vora 2022) show timing-dependent striatal/motor divergence without fine manual dexterity testing.

No human oral sleep or insomnia trial exists for ground clove (topical dental eugenol and aromatherapy protocols are non-oral). In rats, clove oil inhalation produced NO significant effect on pentobarbital sleep duration (Komori et al. 2006, PMID:16857858, null). Oral ground clove effects on Parkinson's insomnia remain open.

Although eugenol (clove scent) is one of the four classic odors used in INHALED olfactory training (rose, eucalyptus, lemon, clove) for Parkinson's hyposmia (Haehner et al. 2013, PMC3629137; Dou et al. 2025, PMID:41477097, PMC12750363), those trials strictly test INHALATION of a 4-odor essential-oil sniffing kit rather than ORAL consumption of ground culinary clove (unusable exposure route and multi-odor bundle). No study tests whether eating ground clove alters olfactory function in PD.

No human standing-blood-pressure, tilt-table, or orthostatic lightheadedness trial tests oral ground clove in Parkinson's disease. Oral clove polyphenol safety/glycemic pilots (Mohan 2019, PMID:31064377; Mammen 2018, PMID:30234415) did not report orthostatic hypotension, and traditional clove texts note warming/digestive uses rather than postural blood-pressure effects.

No human balance trial tests ground clove in Parkinson's disease, and animal eugenol PD models directly conflict depending on timing: while pre-lesion eugenol protected against MPTP/6-OHDA deficits (Kabuto 2007, PMID:17329831; Vora 2022 pre-treatment, PMID:36002316), POST-lesion oral eugenol WORSENED beam-crossing balance/akinesia in MPTP mice (Vora 2022) and WORSENED striatal dopamine loss in 6-OHDA mice (Kabuto & Yamanushi 2011, PMID:21769642). Hamdi 2025 (PMC12767442) tested clove essential oil only in vitro in cells. Because post-lesion worsening contradicts pre-lesion benefit, postural instability remains open with a timing-safety warning.

No human clinical trial or tremor-specific animal assay tests oral ground clove on Parkinson's rest tremor. Preclinical eugenol PD models (Kabuto 2007 vs Kabuto & Yamanushi 2011; Vora 2022) diverge sharply between pre-lesion protection and post-lesion dopaminergic/motor worsening without quantifying rest tremor.

No human gait-kinematics trial or rodent stride-length assay tests ground clove. Animal eugenol PD experiments (Vora 2022, PMID:36002316; Kabuto & Yamanushi 2011, PMID:21769642) diverge between pre-lesion protection and post-lesion worsening without measuring stride length.
No human micrographia or handwriting kinematics trial evaluates ground clove in Parkinson's disease.

No clinical swallowing trial tests culinary ground clove in Parkinson's disease. Two non-dietary clove-oil records provide distinct contextual boundaries: Lomi et al. 2024 (n=134) showed a pre-intubation topical clove-oil gargle reduced postoperative sore throat (not PD dysphagia or oral spice), whereas AlBaazi & Hassoun 2022 reported a single non-PD diabetic man who developed transient dysphagia, dysarthria, and fasciculations roughly two weeks after repeated concentrated clove oil ingestion (unverified causation, concentrated oil rather than culinary ground clove). A 2009 Parkinson's UK forum post mentioned holding a whole clove in the mouth for drooling without reporting swallowing outcomes.
No human clinical trial, observational Parkinson's psychosis cohort, or animal visual-hallucination study evaluates ground clove.

No human walking-speed trial tests ground clove in Parkinson's disease, and rodent eugenol PD models directly contradict one another depending on lesion timing: pre-lesion eugenol attenuated 6-OHDA/MPTP deficits (Kabuto 2007, PMID:17329831; Vora 2022 pre-treatment, PMID:36002316), whereas POST-lesion oral eugenol WORSENED striatal dopamine loss (Kabuto & Yamanushi 2011, PMID:21769642) and WORSENED MPTP akinesia/beam traversal (Vora 2022 post-treatment). Because post-lesion animal harm opposes pre-lesion protection and zero human PD gait trials exist, walking slowness remains open.

Consistent with all 12 Round 1 coconut oil adjudications (all open), no controlled human trial isolates virgin coconut oil for anxiety severity in or outside Parkinson disease. Platero et al. 2020 (PMID:31979305, NCT03740295, n=51 multiple sclerosis patients) reported lower STAI state anxiety, BUT bundled 60 mL/day coconut oil with 800 mg/day EGCG and an isocaloric Mediterranean diet (unusable attribution for isolated coconut oil). Law et al. 2014 (PMID:25163649, PMC4176590, n=60 breast cancer chemotherapy) was an open-label no-placebo study measuring a composite EORTC emotional-functioning score rather than a validated anxiety scale. Non-PD rodent stress/toxin studies (Vasconcelos 2023 PMID:37318515, Asuku 2022) do not model Parkinson anxiety, and MVP observational PD cohorts (PMID:29081890, 2026 preprint) report composite PRO-PD without oil grade or an adjusted anxiety estimate.

Consistent with Round 1 claim 0598 (refined coconut oil and executive function = open), direct randomized human trials testing coconut oil on attention and global cognition are null or confounded: Diekmann et al. 2026 (PMID:41232773, PMC12881678, n=29 older adults with cardiometabolic risk, 4-way crossover of 25 g/50 g cold-pressed virgin coconut oil vs canola oil) found NO difference between coconut oil and canola oil on the Frankfurt Attention Inventory-2 K score (-3, 95% CI -14 to 9, p=0.632; net iAUC p=0.278) or VVM memory; Fernando et al. 2023 (VCO-AD, PMID:37980665, n=120 mild-to-moderate AD, 24-week DB-RCT of 30 mL/day VCO vs canola oil) found NO overall difference in MMSE or Clock Drawing (subgroup APOE e4+ p=0.021 only; 30% attrition); de la Rubia Orti et al. 2018 (PMID:30056419, n=44 AD 21-day pilot) bundled coconut oil into a Mediterranean diet without an isolated attention test or refined grade; DICE pilot (NCT03727386) showed slower switching on EVCO vs sunflower oil (p=0.037); and Karr et al. 2012 (PMID:22250656, n=41) used coconut oil as a placebo arm with TMT learning effects. Parkinson UK forum accounts (2013) include a 4-month no-benefit self-report alongside caregiver anecdotes (Newport 2024).

No human clinical trial isolates refined coconut oil on bradykinesia severity in Parkinson disease. Ketogenic/MCT Parkinson trials (Phillips 2018 PMID:30098269, Choi 2024 PMC10983636, Tosefsky 2026 KIM PMC13347592) tested whole ketogenic diets or fractionated C8/C10 MCT oil rather than refined whole coconut oil (~50% lauric acid C12) and showed no between-diet MDS-UPDRS Part III bradykinesia superiority. Preclinical rat models tested traditional Kerala hot-processed virgin coconut oil (Deepika 2026 PMID:42217587, abstract omitting specific motor test names/means/p-values) or isolated lauric acid with coconut oil as vehicle (Zaidi 2020 PMID:32863249). MVP observational cohorts model total PRO-PD without refined grade or bradykinesia isolation.

No controlled clinical trial demonstrates that virgin coconut oil reduces constipation severity in Parkinson disease or chronic constipation. In Law et al. 2014 (PMID:25163649, PMC4176590, n=60 breast cancer chemotherapy), Table 3 explicitly showed NO statistically significant between-group difference on EORTC QLQ-C30 constipation at any cycle (VCO 31.16 to 40.86 vs control 28.75 to 41.38, NS). Chinwong et al. 2017 (PMID:29387131, n=32 healthy adults, 30 mL/day oral VCO) noted mild diarrhea as a tolerability adverse event rather than a constipation trial, and Tosefsky et al. 2026 (KIM PD MeDi-MCT) logged 2 diarrhea events without an isolated VCO constipation contrast. A 2012 Parkinson UK thread noted constipation as a concern on ketogenic high-fat diets.

No controlled human trial isolates virgin coconut oil for depressive symptom severity in or outside Parkinson disease. In the only double-blind MDD RCT administering coconut oil alone (Mozaffari-Khosravi et al. 2013, PMID:22910528, n=62 analyzed), low-dose coconut oil served as the placebo arm with 0 treatment responders vs 6 responders on EPA (HAM-D p=0.002). Platero et al. 2021 (PMID:33920655, NCT03740295, same n=51 MS cohort as Platero 2020) lowered BDI-II scores using 60 mL coconut oil BUNDLED with 800 mg/day EGCG and a Mediterranean diet (unusable attribution for isolated coconut oil). Non-PD obese/CUMS rodent experiments (Vasconcelos 2023 PMID:37318515, Yeap 2015, Edem 2021) do not establish clinical human Parkinson depression efficacy.

No human clinical trial tests ingested refined coconut oil on Parkinson drooling (sialorrhea). Oral-rinse periodontitis research (Pardinas Lopez et al. 2026, PMID:42057009, n=30 triple-blind pilot) found non-ingested coconut oil mouth rinsing reduced MOUTH DRYNESS perception (p<0.001)—the opposite symptom of drooling—and a 2013 Parkinson UK forum member likewise noted coconut oil helped dry mouth/nose without reporting reduced drooling.

No human Parkinson disease trial or animal dystonia study isolates virgin coconut oil for dystonia severity. Preclinical rodent work tested VCO alongside toxic-dose levodopa in healthy rats (Shehata 2020, PMID:32707436) and traditional hot-processed VCO in rotenone rats (Deepika 2026, PMID:42217587) without dystonia scoring, and PD ketogenic/MCT diets (Phillips 2018, Tosefsky 2026) do not isolate virgin coconut oil or measure dystonia.

No human Parkinson disease trial isolates virgin coconut oil for freezing of gait (FOG) frequency. Whole-diet ketogenic PD trials (Phillips 2018, Choi 2024, Tosefsky 2026) did not isolate virgin coconut oil or demonstrate FOG reduction, and the MS EGCG + 60 mL EVCO trial (Cuerda-Ballester 2023, PMID:36594273) bundled EGCG and tested MS gait speed/balance rather than Parkinson FOG.

No controlled clinical trial isolates refined coconut oil on fine hand dexterity in Parkinson disease. A single 2012 Parkinson UK forum participant taking ~1 teaspoon/week of unspecified coconut oil perceived better hand dexterity and coordination, whereas another participant in the same thread experienced severe acute PD worsening on a ketogenic fat regimen and a 2013 participant saw zero benefit after 4 months. Unverified, conflicting forum accounts without oil grade or objective pegboard testing leave refined coconut oil and hand dexterity open.

No controlled clinical trial tests refined coconut oil on insomnia severity in or outside Parkinson disease. In Law et al. 2014 (PMID:25163649, PMC4176590, n=60 breast cancer chemotherapy), oral virgin coconut oil (not refined) had marked baseline imbalance on EORTC sleep difficulties (36.55 vs 24.12) and Table 3 explicitly confirmed NO statistically significant between-group difference at any cycle. Aromatherapy RCTs (Hu 2026 PMID:41499426, Shammas 2021 PMID:33548936) used fractionated/coconut oil strictly as a non-ingested placebo comparator vs lavender oil.

Consistent with Round 1 claim 0963 (refined coconut oil and speech intelligibility = open), no controlled trial isolates refined coconut oil for hypophonia or low voice volume severity in Parkinson disease. Whole-diet ketogenic voice studies (PMID:32892250, VHI-10) did not assign coconut oil or measure acoustic loudness, and MVP observational cohorts report total PRO-PD without oil grade or voice-volume estimates.

No controlled clinical trial isolates refined coconut oil on Parkinson muscle rigidity severity. In Phillips et al. 2018 (PMID:30098269, n=47 PD randomized), intermittent exacerbation of tremor, rigidity, or both occurred more often during weeks 1-4 on a ketogenic meal plan (12/24 vs 3/23 low-fat; 7/24 vs 5/23 weeks 5-8), but this tested an entire carbohydrate-restricted ketogenic diet (with virgin oil in menus, not refined oil) and pooled tremor/rigidity without isolating coconut oil. Preclinical rotenone rat work (Deepika 2026) tested traditional Kerala hot-processed VCO without rigidity scoring.

Consistent with Round 1 claim 0031, no human clinical trial tests ingesting virgin coconut oil on hyposmia or olfactory impairment in Parkinson disease. The Taichung Parkinson study (PMID:39841404, n=97) used coconut-scented odor identification strips with zero coconut oil consumption, and canine-athlete dietary fat odor-detection studies (PMID:12893164) do not apply to human PD olfaction.

No controlled clinical trial demonstrates an effect of INGESTED virgin coconut oil on Parkinson or chronic systemic pain severity. In Law et al. 2014 (PMID:25163649, PMC4176590, n=60 breast cancer chemotherapy), oral VCO 20 mL/day showed NO statistically significant between-group difference on EORTC QLQ-C30 pain at any cycle (Table 3: 34.03 to 34.94 vs 28.16 to 41.95, NS). Human RCTs reporting pain relief used strictly NON-INGESTED topical or swish-and-spit routes: topical VCO for postpartum nipple fissures (Alikamali 2023 PMID:36638195 n=106 p<0.001; Sahin 2023 PMID:36763614 n=90), topical palatal surgical dressing (Yilmaz 2025 PMID:40858855 n=50), and non-ingested oil-pulling mouth rinse for radiation oral mucositis (Agarwal 2025 PMID:41054470 n=127 p<0.001). Phillips et al. 2018 (PMID:30098269) improved MDS-UPDRS Part 1 pain on a whole ketogenic PD diet without isolating VCO, and preclinical oral VCO rodent analgesia assays (Intahphuak 2010 PMID:20645831, Zakaria 2011) are non-PD writhing/hot-plate models.
No human clinical trial, observational study, or Parkinson community account evaluates refined coconut oil on hypomimia or reduced facial expressiveness.

No controlled clinical trial isolates refined coconut oil for rest tremor severity in Parkinson disease. Phillips et al. 2018 (PMID:30098269, n=47 PD) documented intermittent tremor and/or rigidity exacerbations in 12/24 ketogenic vs 3/23 low-fat participants during weeks 1-4, and Tosefsky et al. 2026 (KIM, PMC13347592) logged 1 exacerbated tremor adverse event during MeDi-MCT, but both tested whole ketogenic diets or fractionated MCT oil rather than refined whole coconut oil and did not report isolated rest-tremor scale comparisons. Preclinical rotenone rat studies (Deepika 2026) tested traditional Kerala hot-processed VCO without tremor measurements.

No human clinical trial isolates virgin coconut oil on stride length in Parkinson disease. Cuerda-Ballester et al. 2023 (PMID:36594273, n=51 MS) bundled 60 mL extra-virgin coconut oil with 800 mg/day EGCG and measured 10MWT gait speed (not stride length) using within-arm tests only, while PD ketogenic/MCT trials (Choi 2024, Tosefsky 2026) did not isolate virgin coconut oil or measure stride length.

No controlled clinical trial evaluates virgin coconut oil on micrographia or small handwriting severity in Parkinson disease. MVP observational baseline heatmaps and total PRO-PD regressions (Mischley 2017, 2023, 2024, 2026 preprint) provide no virgin-grade confirmation or quantified handwriting-item effect estimate.

No clinical trial evaluates virgin coconut oil on oropharyngeal dysphagia or swallowing difficulty severity in Parkinson disease. Vitamin-D fortified lipid drink studies (McCourt et al. 2023, PMID:36912075, n=63) noted liquid fortification could help patients with dysphagia in discussion without enrolling dysphagic patients or testing swallowing mechanics.

No human clinical trial, cohort study, or Parkinson community report tests virgin coconut oil on visual hallucination frequency. The 24-week VCO-AD dementia DB-RCT (Fernando 2023, PMID:37980665, n=120) assessed MMSE, Clock Drawing, and metabolic safety without reporting visual hallucination outcomes.

Consistent with Round 1 claim 0110 (refined coconut oil and postural instability = open), no controlled trial isolates refined coconut oil for walking slowness in Parkinson disease. Choi et al. 2024 (PMID:38561682, PMC10983636, n=15 PD) found NO significant Timed Up & Go (TUG) mobility difference on an MCT-supplemented ketogenic diet vs standard diet. Cuerda-Ballester et al. 2023 (PMID:36594273, n=51 MS) reported within-arm 10MWT gait-speed gains, BUT bundled 60 mL extra-virgin coconut oil with 800 mg/day EGCG and a Mediterranean diet in non-PD MS patients without between-arm change estimates. Parkinson UK forum threads (2012, 2013) preserve conflicting mobility anecdotes (perceived mobility gain in porridge vs acute ketogenic worsening and 4-month no-benefit) alongside community debates over refined seed oils vs coconut oil (HealthUnlocked 2025).
