Multiple controlled non-PD trials—including a direct brewed-coffee crossover (Haskell-Ramsay 2018, n=59, jitteriness p=0.046 in young women and higher in older men vs decaf), a 379-participant double-blind caffeine RCT (Rogers 2010), and Ramirez-delaCruz 2024 (n=29, nervousness p=0.001)—alongside three meta-analyses (Zhang 2026 SMD 0.51, >200 mg SMD 0.97; Liu 2024 SMD 0.94; Klevebrant 2022) show anxiogenic worsening rather than reduction. Because diagnosed PD trials (Postuma 2012, Postuma 2017) and PD cohorts (Sauerbier 2018, Gabbert 2023) observed null anxiety contrasts and Staack 2022 (n=56 OAB women) found lower BAI, the directional lean stays capped at minimal_signal for worsening.

Although Cho 2018 (n=196 drug-naive PD cross-sectional) reported lower adjusted prevalence of lack of motivation and lower NMSS mood/cognition scores (p=0.003) among coffee drinkers, cross-sectional reverse causation (apathetic patients drinking less coffee) cannot be ruled out, Sauerbier 2018 (n=139 PD) found null NMSS mood/apathy differences, Postuma 2012/2017 did not isolate apathy, and Ataka 2008 (n=18 controlled trial) showed null caffeine effects on motivation. Without controlled apathy evidence, the claim remains open.

Sharma 2022 (PMID:35006304, PMC8799544) directly evaluated diagnosed PD participants (n=24 PD + n=42 elderly controls) on standardized attention paradigms (CRT, Stroop, RSVP) after 7-day washout, finding significant reductions in CRT errors (F=4.00, p=0.049) and Stroop errors (F=5.89, p=0.018) with faster Stroop RT (p=0.049) and no adverse disease-by-drug interaction (F<1; p=0.27); because it delivered 100 mg caffeine dissolved in instant decaf coffee rather than freshly brewed coffee and impaired single-item RSVP (p=0.044), exposure_fit and reliability_fit are partial, qualifying for limited_clinical_link (51). Direct brewed-coffee RCTs in healthy adults (Haskell-Ramsay 2018 digit vigilance RT p=0.009, accuracy vs decaf p=0.01; Han 2020 d2 errors; Hindmarch 1998/2000) reinforce the easing signal, tempered by Akyurek 2024 (n=48 null) and Postuma 2017 global MoCA (-0.66 pts).

No human clinical study isolates decaffeinated coffee on bradykinesia severity in Parkinson's disease. Because decaffeination removes the primary A2A antagonist caffeine, isolated caffeine RCTs (Postuma 2012/2017) have unusable exposure transfer. Preclinical mouse alpha-synuclein work on coffee EHT (Lee 2011; Yan 2018) evaluated neuroprotection/synergy with caffeine rather than clinical bradykinesia, and UK Biobank cohort analysis (Zhang 2024) found decaffeinated coffee null for PD incidence. Remains open.

Three controlled human studies directly testing decaffeinated coffee versus water support a caffeine-independent gastrocolic easing signal: Dulskas 2015 (n=90 randomized colectomy trial, time to first bowel movement 3.00 vs 4.14 d water, p<0.05), Rao 1998 (n=12 colonic manometry crossover, pressure waves p<0.01 and propagated contractions p<0.05), and Brown 1990 (n=14, rectosigmoid motility p<0.05 in 8/14 responders), corroborated by Watanabe 2021 meta-analysis (13 RCTs). However, Nasseri 2023 (n=99 colectomy RCT) was null (2.58 vs 2.94 d, p=0.53), Kong 2024 (NHANES n=7,844) found decaf null for chronic constipation, and no Parkinson's trial exists, capping evidence at minimal_signal.

Deleu 2006 (PMID:16966563, n=12 PD double-blind crossover; bridged to brewed coffee via Haskell-Ramsay 2018 and Jeon 2019 HPLC) showed caffeine administered before levodopa shortened levodopa Tmax and reduced latency to walking and tapping motor response (delayed-ON proxy; outcome_fit=partial, exposure_fit=partial), opposing the claim that brewed coffee worsens daily OFF time. Because no trial measured 24-hour patient-diary OFF hours under brewed coffee, Moccia 2016 (n=79) was null on UPDRS-IV, and Postuma 2017 (n=118) worsened dyskinesia without reducing OFF time, the signal is capped at minimal_signal.

Two double-blind placebo-controlled PD trials directly measured daytime sleepiness under caffeine capsules (Postuma 2012 n=61 CGI-C +0.64, PP ESS -1.97; Postuma 2017 n=118 6-mo MDS-UPDRS 1.8 -0.49 and 3-mo SCOPA-sleep daytime -1.09), directly opposing worsening and qualifying for limited_clinical_link (51) when bridged to brewed coffee via Haskell-Ramsay 2018 (100 mg caffeine/220 mL brewed coffee; alertness p<0.0005, tiredness p<0.0001) and Jeon 2019 HPLC. Attenuation over 12-18 mo in Café-PD, mixed responses in Ferreira 2016 (n=4 PD espresso n-of-1), and capsule rather than brewed-coffee PD delivery preclude direct_clinical_signal.

Available human studies isolate regular decaffeinated coffee and show null mood/depression signals: Lucas 2011 (NHS n=50,739, 10-year cohort) observed no reduction in clinical depression risk with decaffeinated coffee (unlike caffeinated coffee), Haskell-Ramsay 2018 (n=59 crossover) found regular decaffeinated coffee did not significantly outperform placebo on overall mood, and Cropley 2012 (n=39) reported acute mood-item differences only with a specialized chlorogenic-acid-enriched decaf blend vs regular decaf. No Parkinson's trial exists, leaving the claim open.

No randomized or controlled clinical study measures dream enactment behavior (DEB) frequency under brewed coffee or caffeine in Parkinson's disease. Jun 2022 (PMID:36187325, PMC9519124, n=96 PSG-confirmed iRBD) asked patients about perceived triggers and found 25/96 (26.0%) endorsed caffeine as aggravating DEBs while 74% did not (subjective retrospective survey without coffee-specific intake or control arm), and Arnaldi 2017 (review) notes epidemiological caffeine protection seen in PD does not hold for iRBD. Remains open.

Controlled and large-cohort evidence shows null signals for drooling/salivary flow: Gabbert 2023 (PMC10260917, n=4,892 PD) found no statistically significant association between binary coffee drinking (p=0.0823), weekly cups (p=0.9754), or duration (p=0.9591) and self-reported saliva/drooling problems, while Hildebrandt 2013 (n=35 crossover) found no significant difference in salivary flow rate between caffeinated and non-caffeinated drinks. Remains open.

Café-PD (Postuma 2017, PMID:28954882, n=118 analyzed PD) directly assessed dyskinesia severity in diagnosed human PD under double-blind randomized caffeine capsules, demonstrating statistically significant worsening on MDS-UPDRS 4.1+4.2 (+0.25 pts combined, 95% CI 0.04-0.45; +0.28 at 3 mo; +0.36 at 18 mo), supported by Shoulson & Chase 1975 (n=6 PD) and bridged to brewed coffee via Haskell-Ramsay 2018 (100 mg/220 mL) and Jeon 2019 HPLC. Because PD trials administered isolated caffeine capsules rather than brewed coffee, and Postuma 2012 (6 wk, few dyskinetic subjects) and Wills 2013 (observational HR 0.61, CI crossing 1.0) did not show worsening, evidence qualifies for limited_clinical_link (51) for worsening.

Targeted searches across Oracle, PubMed, and trial registries found zero clinical or preclinical studies assessing decaffeinated coffee on dystonia severity in Parkinson's disease. UK Biobank incidence analysis (Zhang 2024) evaluated PD diagnosis risk (null for decaf) rather than dystonia severity, and Ferreira 2016 used decaf espresso solely as a somnolence comparator. Remains open.

In the only direct PD cognitive crossover trial (Sharma 2022, PMC8799544, n=24 PD + 42 controls), caffeine improved general response-selection accuracy equally on congruent and incongruent Stroop trials with NO selective Stroop executive-inhibition effect (task-by-drug F<1). Todorovic 2021 (n=16) found caffeine alone null on Trail Making Test A/B, Postuma 2017 (n=118 PD) saw a small decline on global MoCA (-0.66, 95% CI -1.32 to -0.01) without separating executive subscores, and observational cohorts conflict (Cornelis 2020 UKB worse TMT-B vs Zhang 2026 JAMA lower dementia risk/higher global TICS in non-PD adults). Without a clear directional executive-function signal, the claim remains open.

No clinical study measures fall frequency following decaffeinated coffee consumption in Parkinson's disease. Richardson 2024 (n=22 older adults, 68 +/- 6 y) found decaffeinated coffee did not alter standing postural sway or functional mobility compared with placebo or no-fluid control, and UK Biobank cohort data (Zhang 2024) assessed PD incidence rather than falls. Remains open.

Kitagawa 2007 (PMID:17373724) directly observed easing of total-akinesia freezing of gait in diagnosed PD patients taking 100 mg/day oral caffeine (bridged to brewed coffee via Jeon 2019 HPLC and Haskell-Ramsay 2018), matching Round 2 black tea precedent 0627. Uncontrolled design and missing quantitative metrics/n in the indexed abstract force reliability_fit=remote, capping the signal at minimal_signal, further tempered by null Fox Insight freezing regression in Gabbert 2023 (n=4,889, p=0.2364) and null general UPDRS gait items in Postuma 2012/2017.

Direct brewed-coffee testing on fine manual dexterity was null in Gerdes 2022 (PMC9001621, n=107 DB RCT, 340 mL brewed caffeinated vs decaf coffee, p=0.079/p=0.511), and Fuller 2021 (n=49) found overall nine-hole peg test performance unchanged. Opposite acute motor-speed proxies (Deleu 2006 n=12 PD finger-tapping onset latency after levodopa; Fagan 1988 n=18 healthy tapping rate) measure gross tapping speed rather than fine dexterity and are counterbalanced by clinical and community reports of caffeine-provoked hand tremor. Remains open.

Direct brewed-coffee randomized trials outside PD establish sleep-disrupting worsening opposing the reduces statement: Marcus 2023 CRAVE (PMID:36947466, n=100 randomized case-crossover, -36 min/night sleep, 95% CI -47 to -25) and Hindmarch 2000 (n=30 brewed coffee crossover, worsened LSEQ onset/duration/quality p<0.001), corroborated by Drake 2013 (400 mg 0-6 h pre-bed p<0.05), Gardiner 2025 (n=23, 400 mg within 12 h delayed sleep onset; 100 mg null), and Pauchon 2024 (n=41, -30.2 min TST p=0.02). In diagnosed PD, Postuma 2017 nighttime sleep point estimates leaned toward worsening with CIs spanning zero (MDS-UPDRS 1.7 +0.28 [-0.06 to 0.62]; SCOPA-nighttime +0.81 [-0.11 to 1.73]; reliability_fit=remote) and Postuma 2012 PSQI was null (-0.29 [-1.42 to 0.84]), capping the tier at minimal_signal.

No clinical trial, observational cohort, or acoustic study tests decaffeinated coffee on vocal intensity or hypophonia in Parkinson's disease. Existing decaf cohort data (Zhang 2024 UK Biobank) evaluate PD incidence only, and Ferreira 2016 used decaf espresso solely as a somnolence placebo. Remains open.

Postuma 2012 (PMID:22855866, n=61 PD double-blind RCT) directly isolated Parkinson's UPDRS-III rigidity and found a statistically significant 6-week reduction (-1.01 pts, 95% CI -2.0 to -0.7), bridged to brewed coffee via Haskell-Ramsay 2018 (100 mg caffeine/220 mL brewed coffee) and Jeon 2019 HPLC. Because the PD RCT administered isolated caffeine capsules rather than brewed coffee (exposure_fit=partial) and the longer 6-18 month Café-PD trial (Postuma 2017, n=118) showed null total motor MDS-UPDRS III (-0.48, 95% CI -3.21 to 2.25), evidence qualifies for limited_clinical_link (51).

Han 2020 (PMID:30813710, n=49 crossover) compared brewed caffeinated versus decaffeinated coffee and observed no acute olfactory performance difference between beverages despite improved attention on caffeinated coffee, without a non-coffee control or Parkinson's hyposmia cohort. No clinical trial tests decaffeinated coffee on UPSIT or Sniffin' Sticks scores in Parkinson's disease. Remains open.

Controlled hemodynamic studies directly testing decaffeinated coffee show neither clinical orthostatic worsening nor consistent pressor benefit: Nussberger 1990 (n=8) and Lima de Castro 2024 (n=16) found no BP change vs water, Heseltine 1991 (n=7 elderly) found decaf lacked caffeinated coffee's protection against postprandial BP drop, Aoun 2021 (n=139 hemodialysis RCT) found identical intradialytic hypotension between decaf (26%) and caffeinated coffee (27%, p=0.539), and Corti 2002 (n=15) measured resting supine BP/MSNA in non-habitual drinkers without orthostatic symptoms. No PD orthostatic-lightheadedness study exists, leaving the claim open.

Direct comparisons of ordinary decaffeinated coffee fail to establish pain reduction: Haskell-Ramsay 2018 (PMC6213082, n=59) showed regular brewed coffee reduced headache vs decaf (p=0.0049) while decaf did not beat placebo, Aoun 2021 (n=139) showed null headache differences (33.3% vs 37.1%, p=0.522), and van Dusseldorp & Katan 1990 showed switching habitual coffee drinkers to decaf triggered withdrawal headaches. Although Camfield 2013 (PMC3857311, n=60) saw lower 120-min VAS headache ratings with a specialized CGA-enriched green-coffee decaf blend (p=0.03), that fortified formulation does not represent ordinary decaffeinated coffee or Parkinson's pain. Remains open.

Controlled human balance trials directly testing decaffeinated coffee yield conflicting results outside Parkinson's disease: Richardson 2024 (PMID:39321752, n=22 older adults, 4-arm crossover with matched placebo and no-fluid control) found decaffeinated coffee had zero effect on standing COP postural stability (p>0.05), whereas Cildir 2021 (PMC8864202, n=15 young adults aged 20-35 in Group 2, allowing milk/sugar/sweeteners after 48-h caffeine abstention without a blinded water placebo) reported lower SOT composite and C5 equilibrium scores (p=0.001) alongside null adaptation-test scores. Without PD testing or replication in older adults, the claim remains open.

No controlled or observational human study assesses decaffeinated coffee on facial expressiveness or hypomimia in Parkinson's disease. Existing decaf cohort data (Zhang 2024 UK Biobank) evaluate PD diagnosis risk only, and Ferreira 2016 used decaf espresso solely as a somnolence comparator. Remains open.

No controlled clinical study tests whether decaffeinated coffee reduces Parkinson's rest tremor relative to water or baseline. Because decaffeination removes caffeine, caffeine-capsule PD trials (Postuma 2012/2017) have unusable exposure transfer. Preclinical EHT models (Lee 2011; Yan 2018) evaluated neuroprotection rather than rest tremor, and community accounts (Parkinson's UK 2024, 2013) discuss decaf only as a way to avoid caffeinated coffee's stimulatory shaking. Remains open.

No human trial isolates stride length after brewed coffee in Parkinson's disease. Postuma 2012 (PMID:22855866, n=61 PD) found non-significant general UPDRS gait item changes (-0.12/-0.28, CIs spanning zero), Postuma 2017 (n=118) showed null total motor scores, Gabbert 2023 (n=4,889 PD) found null walking/balance association (p=0.1156), and Marcus 2023 (n=100) measured daily step volume (+1,058 steps/d) rather than stride shortening. Remains open.

Targeted searches found no human clinical trial or Parkinson's cohort measuring handwriting size or micrographia under brewed coffee or caffeine. Major PD caffeine RCTs (Postuma 2012 n=61; Postuma 2017 n=118) did not isolate handwriting items, and brewed-coffee dexterity testing outside PD (Gerdes 2022, n=107) was null on fine motor precision. Remains open.

No randomized trial evaluates brewed coffee or caffeine on listener-rated speech intelligibility or dysarthria in Parkinson's disease. Fox Insight regression in 4,892 PD participants (Gabbert 2023, PMC10260917) found null associations for coffee use (p=0.1615), weekly cups (p=0.7086), and duration (p=0.2585), while Postuma 2012/2017 did not isolate speech intelligibility. Remains open.

Available evidence is indirect and confounded: in Gabbert 2023 (PMC10260917, n=4,892 PD), binary coffee drinking was marginally linked to fewer chewing/swallowing complaints (p=0.0497, beta=-0.1435) but weekly dosage (p=0.6961) and duration (p=0.4785) were completely null, fitting reverse causation where dysphagic PD patients drink fewer thin liquids/coffee (consistent with Cassani 2017, n=600 PD vs 600 controls). Conversely, Lohsiriwat 2006 (n=12 healthy) found 3.5 mg/kg caffeine lowered lower-esophageal-sphincter pressure and distal esophageal peristalsis (reflux proxy, not PD oropharyngeal dysphagia). Remains open.

Controlled urinary symptom RCTs outside PD demonstrate urgency worsening from caffeinated beverages: Wells 2014 (PMID:24988515, n=11 completed OAB women DB crossover, urgency p<0.01, frequency p<0.05, ICIQ-OAB p<0.01) and Bryant 2002 (PMID:11979209, n=95 continence RCT, urgency p=0.002, frequency p=0.037), corroborated by NHANES (Gleason 2013, n=4,309) and Park 2023 systematic review. Because no Parkinson's-specific bladder trial exists, Swithinbank 2005 (n=69 women crossover) found caffeine restriction null, Ha 2025 noted mixed evidence, and Sauerbier 2018 (n=139 PD) showed null NMSS urinary scores, evidence is capped at minimal_signal.

Available studies show null associations rather than worsening or easing: Agoston 2022 (PMID:34792804, n=181 DB RCT) found 100 mg caffeine did not increase experimental hallucination-like experiences (unlike acute stress), Agoston 2018 (n=2,259 survey) found no correlation between coffee/caffeine intake and psychosis-like symptoms, and Sauerbier 2018 (PMC6312592, n=139 PD) found null NMSS perceptual/hallucination domain differences. No PD visual-hallucination trial exists, leaving the claim open.

Three controlled human trials point toward faster walking rather than worsening slowness: Deleu 2006 (PMID:16966563, n=12 PD DB crossover, increased walking response magnitude and shorter walking-onset latency after levodopa; reliability_fit=remote because abstract omits exact walking effect size/CI), Marinho 2024 (n=15 older adults crossover, 10-m walk p=0.008 & TUG p=0.002), and Waer 2024 (n=85 RCT, 100 mg/d caffeine improved 10-m walk speed p<0.05), bridged to brewed coffee via Jeon 2019 HPLC. Tempered by null gait/mobility trials (Richardson 2024 n=22 brewed coffee; Norager 2005 n=30 elderly; Postuma 2012 UPDRS gait; Gabbert 2023 n=4,889 walking/balance p=0.1156), evidence stays at minimal_signal for easing.

Evidence remains open for refined corn oil worsening anxiety severity in Parkinson disease. In Parkinson and adult human trials, corn oil functioned strictly as an inert placebo capsule or shared cannabidiol (CBD) carrier rather than an isolated dietary intervention: de Faria et al. 2020 (PMID:31909680, n=24 PD crossover) administered CBD in corn oil versus matching corn-oil vehicle before public speaking (measuring CBD efficacy rather than corn-oil harm, with no oil-free arm), and Crippa et al. 2022 (PMID:34076067) found null anxiety differences across CBD formulations dissolved in corn oil vs corn-oil placebo. Public PD community discussions reflect polarized cautionary anti-seed-oil sentiment (HealthUnlocked Sept 2025) balanced by community skepticism noting the absence of PD seed-oil trials (HealthUnlocked Oct 2025).

Evidence remains open for refined corn oil worsening daily OFF time in Parkinson disease. No clinical trial isolates dietary refined corn oil on levodopa pharmacokinetics or daily OFF time. Chagas et al. 2014 (PMID:25237116, n=21 PD) used corn-oil gelatin capsules as a shared CBD carrier/placebo across all arms without reporting OFF-time outcomes. Existing human cucumber studies—such as Hausenblas et al. 2025 (PMID:40636535, n=80 Q-Actin mood/sleep/fatigue, all Group x Time null), Ji et al. 2015 (PMID:26193861, n=30 antioxidant markers), and traditional Ayurvedic/Unani cooling accounts (Mukherjee 2013)—did not test this Parkinson endpoint.

Evidence remains open for pickled cucumber worsening orthostatic lightheadedness severity in Parkinson disease. No clinical study tests pickled cucumber on supine-to-standing blood pressure or orthostatic symptoms in Parkinson disease. Galena et al. 2022 (PMID:36201455, local extract) bundled fermented/pickled cabbage and/or cucumber and reported non-significant seated blood pressure differences (p=0.093) without orthostatic challenge, while sodium content in commercial pickled cucumbers (~200 mg per two small pickles noted in Cure Parkinson's HealthUnlocked 2013) would physiologically tend toward plasma volume expansion rather than orthostatic drop, though unstudied clinically in PD neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

Two distinct human clinical pain streams outside Parkinson disease lean toward pain easing rather than worsening, with zero controlled trials showing cucumber worsens pain, while substantial preparation, attribution, and replication limits cap certainty at minimal_signal (eases — contradicting the frozen worsening hypothesis). First, standardized Cucumis sativus aqueous/hydro-ethanolic fruit extract (Q-Actin, >1% idoBR1) outperformed glucosamine-chondroitin in moderate knee osteoarthritis over 180 days (Nash et al. 2018 PMID:30498336, PMC6207263, n=115 analyzed: WOMAC -70.3% vs -33.7%, VAS pain -46.3% vs -25.6%, p<0.05; sponsor-affiliated active-comparator trial) and outperformed cellulose placebo at 20 mg and 100 mg/day (Nash et al. 2023 PMID:36748212, n=91 completed; same Phytoquest/Nash group; Yan et al. 2025 NMA PMID:41126953 cautions independent replication is needed); an independent 60-day joint-pain RCT of Q-Actin 20 mg/day (Hausenblas et al. 2025 PMID:41040766, PMC12486685, n=80) found non-significant Group x Time interaction on WOMAC (p=0.13) and LFI (p=0.13) with marginal BPI pain interference significance (p=0.05) amid baseline imbalance, alongside mouse aqueous-fruit-extract analgesia (Kumar 2010 PMID:21264095). Second, liquid dill/kosher pickled cucumber brine ('pickle juice') reduced acute painful cirrhotic muscle-cramp VAS severity versus tap water in an open-label RCT (Tapper et al. 2022 PICCLES PMID:35416793, PMC11214544, n=74 analyzed: -2.25 vs -0.36, p=0.03; cramp-days p=0.2) and shortened electrically induced cramp duration in a laboratory crossover (Miller et al. 2010 PMID:19997012, n=10: -49.1 s, p<0.05), though mechanistic analysis attributes rapid reflex inhibition to vinegar acetic acid rather than cucumber phytochemistry (Hooper Marosek 2020 PMID:32459412). Observational migraine trigger surveys rarely implicate cucumber (0.43% of 3,935 patients, Silva-Neto 2021 PMID:33892616), and cultural/community records note traditional Ayurvedic/Unani soothing uses plus mixed Cure Parkinson's HealthUnlocked accounts of dill pickle juice relieving minor cramping versus sodium concerns. Because no trial tests eaten whole pickled cucumbers in diagnosed Parkinson pain, the surviving easing signal remains minimal_signal (eases).

Five independent oral Lavandula angustifolia RCT families support an easing lean on anxiety in non-PD adults: brewed lavender herbal tea reduced STAI state (-6.40) and trait (-4.13) anxiety in older adults (PMID:32444033, n=60), reinforced by four multicenter DB-RCTs of oral standardized lavender oil Silexan 80-160 mg/d in subsyndromal anxiety, GAD, restlessness, and MADD (PMID:20512042, PMID:24456909, PMID:26293583, PMID:26718792). Two null oral RCTs in postmenopausal women (PMID:38754638) and COVID-19 syrup (PMID:37663382), unblinded tea allocation, Silexan-to-tea exposure gaps, and absence of PD clinical trials cap the tier at minimal_signal.

No human clinical or animal study directly tests brewed culinary lavender on apathy severity in Parkinson's disease; in the oral Silexan MDD DB-RCT item analysis (PMID:42550483, n=498), MADRS item 8 ('inability to feel'/anhedonia) was borderline/non-significant vs placebo (-1.25 vs -1.01, p=0.058), while lassitude eased (p=0.003) in non-PD depression using essential oil rather than brewed tea, keeping the claim open.

Objective sustained attention and driving performance with oral Silexan 80-320 mg in healthy adults was equivalent to placebo (PMID:33221027, n=50/25, null), whereas an exploratory unadjusted MADRS item analysis in non-PD MDD reported lower subjective 'concentration difficulties' (-1.40 vs -1.08, p=0.011, PMID:42550483) and inhaled lavender aroma slowed attention reaction times (PMID:12690999, non-oral); with no brewed lavender tea or PD attention trial, the claim remains open.

No clinical or PD animal study evaluates ground Illicium verum on postural instability severity; parenteral i.p. solvent extracts did not alter healthy rodent rotarod coordination (PMID:24083582, non-oral), keeping the claim open.

No clinical or animal study evaluates ground Illicium verum on hypomimia or reduced facial expressiveness in Parkinson's disease; targeted Oracle, PubMed, and registry sweeps found zero facial-expression motor outcomes, keeping the claim open.

No clinical or PD tremor model tests ground Illicium verum on rest tremor severity; pediatric toxicology reports of star anise tea document acute tremors, myoclonus, and seizures driven by Illicium anisatum (anisatin) adulteration or overdose (PMID:12907070, PMID:15492355, PMID:36760188), representing a critical botanical-adulteration safety hazard rather than authentic culinary I. verum rest tremor evidence, keeping the claim open.

No clinical or PD animal gait study evaluates ground Illicium verum on shortened stride severity; only non-oral i.p. rodent locomotion assays (PMID:24083582) and cellular shikimic acid redox work (PMID:25862258) exist, keeping the claim open.

No clinical or preclinical study evaluates ground Illicium verum on micrographia or small handwriting severity in Parkinson's disease; targeted Oracle, PubMed, and registry sweeps found zero handwriting endpoints, keeping the claim open.

No clinical or animal study evaluates ground Illicium verum on speech intelligibility impairment in Parkinson's disease; the only human I. verum RCT tested a topical gingival mouthwash (PMID:34195261, n=50) without assessing articulation or speech, keeping the claim open.

No clinical or animal dysphagia study evaluates ground Illicium verum on swallowing difficulty severity in Parkinson's disease; the topical I. verum mouthwash RCT assessed periodontal indices only (PMID:34195261, n=50), keeping the claim open.

No clinical or animal study evaluates ground Illicium verum on urinary urgency frequency in Parkinson's disease (distinct from Round 2 Pimpinella anisum diuresis data); targeted Oracle, PubMed, and registry sweeps returned zero urinary urgency endpoints, keeping the claim open.

No clinical trial or PD psychosis study evaluates ground Illicium verum on visual hallucination frequency; food-safety LC/DART-MS literature explicitly warns that star anise adulterated with neurotoxic Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum, anisatin) can induce hallucinations, epilepsy, and nausea (PMID:22484123), and mixed star/green anise infant poisoning caused acute seizures and nystagmus (LOCAL:ObandoPacheco2016), documenting an adulteration hazard while leaving authentic ground I. verum open.

No clinical or PD gait study evaluates ground Illicium verum on walking slowness; parenteral i.p. I. verum solvent extracts lowered healthy rodent locomotion (PMID:24083582, non-oral) and oral isolated veranisatin A reduced methamphetamine-stimulated locomotion near convulsant thresholds (PMID:8904818), keeping the claim open.

Strictly evaluating true Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa 'black cumin' and Bunium persicum): Ito et al. 2026 (PMID:42088310, PMC13135935, n=38 analyzed cognitively healthy Japanese older adults) tested steam-distilled cumin essential oil (25 mg cuminaldehyde/d) vs MCT placebo for 12 weeks and found statistically significant group-by-time interactions on Cognitrax Psychomotor Speed (p=0.012) and Reaction Time (p=0.022), BUT isolated Motor Speed (Finger Tapping) was NULL (p=0.093), 5/43 subjects were excluded post-hoc, no multiplicity adjustment was applied across 11 domains, PD was excluded, and steam-distilled oil differs from toasted whole spice. Preclinically, Kim, Kopalli & Koppula 2016 (aqueous C. cyminum in MPTP mice) improved day-20 rotarod and open-field locomotion, but contains an unresolved n=15 vs n=5 sample-size discrepancy (matching Round 1 0474/0596/0967 kept open), and Morshedi 2015 (PMID:26351865) is cell-free alpha-synuclein biochemistry only. Evidence for toasted cumin on Parkinson's bradykinesia remains open.

Strictly evaluating true Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa 'black cumin' depression studies): Ito et al. 2026 (PMID:42088310, PMC13135935, n=38 older adults, 12-week DB-RCT of cumin essential oil softgels) assessed the Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS) and POMS2 mood scales as secondary QoL endpoints and reported NO significant group-by-time interaction (null). No controlled trial of culinary toasted cumin tests Parkinson's depression.

No human polysomnography, REM-sleep behavior disorder (RBD), or dream-enactment study tests true Cuminum cyminum. Mouse pentobarbital sleep prolongation with cumin essential oil (Nouri 2024, PMID:39619952) does not evaluate REM atonia or dream enactment.

No clinical trial tests oral toasted cumin on Parkinson's sialorrhea/drooling. Napavichayanun et al. 2026 (PMID:42208428) tested a TOPICAL herbal artificial-saliva spray containing BOTH Cuminum cyminum AND Zingiber officinale (ginger, a known sialagogue) in hemodialysis patients with xerostomia (dry mouth), observing higher salivary flow (0.06 vs 0.02 g/min, p=0.04) and lower dry-mouth scores (p=0.024). Because the preparation was a topical spray co-formulated with ginger in dry-mouth dialysis patients (not oral toasted cumin in PD sialorrhea), drooling effects remain open.

No human clinical trial or animal dystonia model tests true Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa) for Parkinson's dystonia. Culinary metabolic RCTs of ground cumin powder (Zare 2014, PMID:25456022, n=88 overweight women) measured only anthropometric and lipid parameters.

Full-text Table 4 of Ito et al. 2026 (PMID:42088310, PMC13135935, n=38 analyzed cognitively healthy Japanese older adults, 12-week DB-RCT of cumin essential oil softgels containing 25 mg cuminaldehyde/d) explicitly demonstrated NULL between-group effects on Executive Function (17.3->19.7 vs 24.4->24.9, interaction p=0.629, Cohen's d=0.12) and Cognitive Flexibility (interaction p=0.793), despite exploratory improvements in psychomotor speed and reaction time (local extract 2026-Ito-Cumin-Oil-Attention-Factual-Extract.txt). Preclinical rodent spatial/avoidance memory studies (Omari 2021, PMC7880363 dietary cuminaldehyde in aged mice; Koppula & Choi 2011, PMID:21639683 scopolamine rats) do not measure human executive function, and Nigella sativa studies are strictly excluded. Therefore ground cumin effects on executive function remain open.

No human prospective fall-frequency trial evaluates toasted Cuminum cyminum in Parkinson's disease. An MPTP mouse aqueous-extract study (Kim 2016) carries an unresolved n=15 vs n=5 reporting discrepancy and measured rotarod latency rather than clinical human falls.

Strictly evaluating true Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa): Omidvar et al. 2019 (PMID:31383440) randomized 31 dysmenorrheic young females across three spice arms (ginger 1 g/d, dill 3 g/d, cumin 3 g/d; ~10 per arm, NO placebo comparator) and noted in prose that cumin reduced systemic menstrual symptoms including fatigue, cold sweats, backache, and cramps without reporting validated fatigue scores or placebo-controlled statistics. Meanwhile, Ito et al. 2026 (PMID:42088310, PMC13135935, n=38 older adults) measured POMS2 fatigue/vigor and found NO significant group-by-time interaction (null). Without placebo-controlled or numerical fatigue easing, toasted cumin effects on Parkinson's fatigue remain open.

No human Parkinson's freezing-of-gait trial tests ground Cuminum cyminum. A rotenone fruit-fly climbing experiment (local 2015-2019 cumin record) and an unisolated Ayurvedic combination case including Mucuna pruriens (local 2025-2029 cumin record) do not measure freezing of gait or isolate ground cumin.

In Ito et al. 2026 (PMID:42088310, PMC13135935, n=38 analyzed healthy older adults, 12-week DB-RCT), steam-distilled cumin essential oil (25 mg cuminaldehyde/d) improved composite Cognitrax Psychomotor Speed (Finger Tapping + Symbol Digit Coding, interaction p=0.012) while isolated Motor Speed (Finger Tapping) was NULL (p=0.093) and Trail Making Peg numerical results were unreported. Given the null isolated motor-speed domain, unadjusted 11-domain testing with 5/43 post-hoc exclusions, essential oil softgel vs culinary toasted cumin, and non-PD healthy participants, hand dexterity effects remain open. A 2012 Parkinson's UK forum member shared a Jeera chicken recipe recommending kitchen scissors to accommodate hand dexterity without claiming cumin altered dexterity.

Strictly evaluating true Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa sleep trials): Ito et al. 2026 (PMID:42088310, PMC13135935, n=38 older adults, 12-week DB-RCT of cumin essential oil) evaluated the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) and found NO significant group-by-time interaction (null). Nouri et al. 2024 (PMID:39619952, PMC11606850) showed cumin essential oil prolonged mouse pentobarbital sleeping time—a single rodent barbiturate-potentiation assay tempered by the null human PSQI result. Toasted cumin effects on Parkinson's insomnia remain open.

No clinical or acoustic speech-volume trial tests ground Cuminum cyminum for Parkinson's hypophonia. Boominathan et al. 2026 (PMID:38030481, J Voice) documented traditional Tamil 'Paati Vaidyam' home remedies used by school teachers for voice disorders—including cumin seeds alongside pepper, ginger, and honey—providing verified customary cultural context without any efficacy or acoustic loudness measurement.

No human olfactory-testing or Parkinson's hyposmia trial evaluates toasted Cuminum cyminum. A 2018 Parkinson's UK forum contributor recommended aromatic non-chili spices including cumin and coriander to enhance meal flavor during PD taste changes without claiming restored smell thresholds.

Minimal directional lean toward easing pain (Maybe False, 50.005, opposing the frozen 'worsens' claim), strictly restricted to true Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa): Amin et al. 2024 (PMID:38965524, PMC11229490, n=72 analyzed, triple-blind placebo-controlled RCT) demonstrated oral C. cyminum hydroalcoholic extract capsules (250 mg x 2) significantly lowered acute postoperative abdominal pain frequency vs starch placebo at 6-8 h (12 vs 21, p=0.03), 14-16 h (13 vs 22, p=0.03), and 16-18 h (4 vs 16, p<0.01; null at other 2-h windows), corroborated preclinically by Nouri 2024 (PMID:39619952, cumin EO acetic-acid writhing), Koohsari 2020 (PMID:32222574, cuminaldehyde nociceptive and CCI neuropathic pain), and Sheikholeslami 2021 (PMID:33811835, cuminic alcohol), plus uncontrolled IBS abdominal-pain relief in Agah 2013 (PMID:24829694, n=57, single-arm only -> claim_effect=none). Transparently tempered by null results in Omidvar 2019 (PMID:31383440, n=31 3-arm non-placebo dysmenorrhea pain null), Haghparast 2008 (PMID:18550281, mouse tail-flick EO null), and Golabi 2022 (PMID:35280043, raw rat seed extract formalin null)—with ZERO trials showing cumin worsens pain. Non-PD acute surgical pain, extract capsules vs ground spice, and competing nulls cap confidence strictly at minimal_signal.
No human clinical trial or observational Parkinson's study evaluates toasted cumin on hypomimia (reduced facial expressiveness).

No human clinical trial or tremor-specific animal experiment tests true ground Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa) on Parkinson's rest tremor. Kim 2016 (MPTP mouse rotarod/open-field with n=15 vs n=5 discrepancy) and Morshedi 2015 (in vitro alpha-synuclein) did not measure rest tremor.

No human gait-kinematics trial or rodent stride-length assay tests true ground Cuminum cyminum. Kim 2016 (MPTP mouse aqueous extract, n=15 vs n=5 discrepancy) did not measure footprint stride length, and rat GI-transit studies of powdered cumin (local 2000-2004 record) did not assess gait.
No clinical micrographia or handwriting study tests toasted Cuminum cyminum in Parkinson's disease.

No human dysarthria or listener-rated speech intelligibility trial evaluates toasted Cuminum cyminum. Traditional Tamil vocal home remedies mentioning cumin seeds (Boominathan 2026, PMID:38030481) document customary throat/voice practices among teachers without measuring speech intelligibility or Parkinson's dysarthria.
No human clinical trial, pharmacovigilance series, or Parkinson's psychosis cohort evaluates toasted Cuminum cyminum on visual hallucinations.

Strictly evaluating true Cuminum cyminum (excluding Nigella sativa): no human gait-speed trial tests ground cumin in Parkinson's disease. Ito et al. 2026 (PMID:42088310, PMC13135935, n=38 healthy older adults) measured seated computerized cognition/motor speed (isolated Motor Speed null p=0.093) rather than walking speed, and Kim 2016 (MPTP mouse aqueous extract) carries an unresolved n=15 vs n=5 sample-size discrepancy and did not assess human gait speed—aligning with Round 1 0474/0596/0967 kept open.

Strictly evaluating botanical Murraya koenigii leaves (excluding commercial curry powder blends): human and animal anxiety findings are null or directly conflicting. In humans, Lauche et al. 2016 (PMID:27261998, n=32 IBS-D crossover RCT) tested a bundled 3-herb decoction (M. koenigii + pomegranate + turmeric) and found NULL effects on HADS anxiety (and cannot isolate curry leaf). In mice, Dahiya et al. 2016 (PMID:27737817) reported anxiolytic EPM open-arm increases with hydroalcoholic extract and isolated mahanimbine, whereas Sharma et al. 2017 (PMID:29269974, PMC5726189) found oral aqueous M. koenigii leaf extract REDUCED EPM open-arm entries and locomotor activity (no anxiolytic effect; sedative). Conflicting rodent results plus a null bundled human trial leave anxiety effects open.

No human clinical trial or animal apathy/motivation assay tests cooked Murraya koenigii leaves in Parkinson's disease. Traditional Ayurvedic/Siddha food-medicine records and a 2024 Parkinson's UK cauliflower upma recipe document everyday culinary use without apathy outcomes.

Strict botanical matrix exclusion removes Ng et al. 2006 (PMID:16870699, Singapore elderly cognitive cohort), which measured habitual 'curry' dish intake framed around turmeric/curcumin multi-spice curry powder blends rather than botanical Murraya koenigii leaves. Preclinical M. koenigii leaf rodent studies (Vasudevan & Parle 2009, PMID:18844259, 2-8% dietary leaves; Mani 2012, PMID:22142688 alkaloidal extract; Mani 2021, PMID:35053756 isolated mahanimbine; Bhupatiraju 2023, PMID:36937470 diabetic rat brain aging) evaluated spatial/avoidance memory and AChE inhibition rather than clinical human attention (Stroop, CPT, Digit Span), with zero human M. koenigii cognitive trials. Evidence remains open.

Evidence for Murraya koenigii leaves on bowel motility is directly contradictory across animal studies and unresolved in humans. In rats, Tembhurne & Sakarkar 2011 (PMID:21849153) found leaf extract ACCELERATED impaired diabetic GI charcoal transit, whereas Ramasamy et al. 2016 (PMID:26631977) found hydroalcoholic leaf extract SLOWED charcoal propulsion (antidiarrheal). In humans, Lauche et al. 2016 (PMID:27261998, n=32 IBS-D) found a bundled 3-herb decoction null on IBS severity (p=0.26), and Patel et al. 2025 (PMID:41287676, PMC12640369, n=96 iron-deficiency anemia) reported unvalidated visit-4 'constipation comfort' perception percentages (89.29% Orgen-I iron-only vs 67.86% placebo) without baseline values, stool counts, or between-group p-values alongside severe text/table contradictions. Constipation effects remain open.

No human or animal study evaluates ground Murraya koenigii leaves for daytime sleepiness (Epworth Sleepiness Scale or wakefulness). In mice, Sharma et al. 2017 (PMID:29269974) noted sedative locomotor suppression with high-dose aqueous leaf extract, which does not support reducing daytime sleepiness.

Evidence for Murraya koenigii leaves on depression is weak, unvalidated, or null in humans and confounded in animals: Lauche et al. 2016 (PMID:27261998, n=32 IBS-D crossover RCT) found a bundled 3-herb M. koenigii decoction NULL on HADS depression; Patel et al. 2025 (PMID:41287676, PMC12640369, n=86 analyzed IDA adults) reported unvalidated visit-4 'joyful' perception (96.42% Orgen-I iron-only vs 85.72% placebo) with NO depression scale, NO baseline, NO p-value, and severe reporting contradictions; Anjum 2025 (rotenone PD mice) showed NO significant marker on tail-suspension immobility; and while Sharma et al. 2017 (PMID:29269974) reported lower mouse FST/TST immobility with aqueous extract, it concurrently depressed open-field locomotion and EPM exploration. Thus depressive symptom effects remain open.
No human polysomnography, REM-sleep behavior disorder (RBD), or dream-enactment study tests ground Murraya koenigii leaves.

No human sialorrhea or salivary-flow trial evaluates ground Murraya koenigii leaves in Parkinson's disease. Oral/periodontal M. koenigii mouthwash trials measure gingival plaque rather than Parkinson's drooling.

No human levodopa-induced Parkinson's dyskinesia (LID) trial tests cooked Murraya koenigii leaves, and preclinical dopaminergic/dyskinesia studies directly conflict by extraction fraction: Patil et al. 2012 reported oral methanolic M. koenigii leaf extract reduced reserpine-induced (PMC3832166) and haloperidol-induced (PMID:22136413) vacuous chewing movements (neuroleptic/tardive orofacial dyskinesia proxies, mechanistically distinct from levodopa-induced PD dyskinesia), WHEREAS Patil & Langade 2021 (local) found petroleum-ether and alkaloid M. koenigii leaf fractions PROLONGED haloperidol catalepsy and REDUCED apomorphine-induced locomotion (anti-dopaminergic action). Consistent with Round 1, dyskinesia remains open.

No human Parkinson's dystonia study tests cooked Murraya koenigii leaves, and preclinical dopaminergic rodent assays show directly conflicting pro- versus anti-dopaminergic responses depending on leaf fraction (Patil 2012 vs Patil & Langade 2021; Reddy 2020) without testing dystonia.

Strict botanical separation excludes Ng et al. 2006 (PMID:16870699, Singapore elderly cohort of turmeric-based curry-powder dishes, NOT Murraya koenigii leaves). Preclinical M. koenigii leaf rodent studies (Vasudevan & Parle 2009, PMID:18844259; Mani 2012, PMID:22142688; Mani 2021, PMID:35053756 isolated mahanimbine; Bhupatiraju 2023, PMID:36937470 diabetic rat brain aging) evaluated spatial/avoidance memory and AChE inhibition rather than human prefrontal executive function, and zero human M. koenigii leaf cognitive trials exist. Executive function effects remain open.

No human prospective fall-frequency trial evaluates cooked Murraya koenigii leaves in Parkinson's disease. Preclinical rodent motor/rotarod studies show inconsistent text/table reporting (Reddy 2020), paywalled methods (Anjum 2025), or opposing catalepsy prolongation (Patil & Langade 2021), and none measure clinical human falls.

Full-text audit of Patel et al. 2025 (PMID:41287676, PMC12640369, NCT06096103, n=96 enrolled / n=86 analyzed adults with iron-deficiency anemia, Hb 8-11 g/dL) reveals why it cannot establish directional fatigue efficacy for cooked culinary curry leaf in PD: (1) participants took a concentrated sponsor water extract (500 mg Orgen-I standardized to 3.6% elemental iron = 18 mg elemental iron/day—~90x the iron in a culinary sprig of cooked curry leaves) specifically to correct iron-deficiency anemia (attribution_fit=remote, exposure_fit=remote); (2) the reported visit-4 'energetic' perception (92.85% iron-only vs 67.85% placebo) came from an unvalidated sponsor questionnaire with NO baseline values, NO validated fatigue scale, and NO between-group p-values; and (3) the published Cureus article contains severe internal statistical contradictions between text and Table 1 (reliability_fit=unusable). Practically, concentrated iron supplements can also chelate oral levodopa in PD if co-ingested. Fatigue effects of cooked curry leaf remain open.

No human fine hand-dexterity trial tests cooked Murraya koenigii leaves in Parkinson's disease. Preclinical animal motor assays (Anjum 2025; Reddy 2020; Patil & Langade 2021) conflict across extracts and do not measure human fine manual dexterity.

No human sleep or insomnia trial evaluates cooked Murraya koenigii leaves. Sharma et al. 2017 (PMID:29269974) noted locomotor sedation in mice given high-dose aqueous leaf extract without measuring sleep architecture or insomnia.
No human olfactory-function or Parkinson's hyposmia study tests ground Murraya koenigii leaves.

No human standing-blood-pressure, tilt-table, or orthostatic lightheadedness study tests ground Murraya koenigii leaves in Parkinson's disease. Gopal et al. 2023 (PMID:37969660, PMC10640786) conducted a non-randomized quasi-experimental pre-post study in rural Indian hypertensive adults reporting lower resting blood pressure after curry leaf intake; resting blood-pressure lowering in hypertension neither measures standing orthostasis nor suggests improvement of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

Minimal directional lean toward easing pain (Maybe False, 50.005, directly opposing the frozen 'worsens' claim): six independent controlled rodent analgesia laboratories testing oral Murraya koenigii leaf extracts across diverse acute inflammatory, central thermal, glutamate, and chronic neuropathic pain models consistently report antinociceptive easing with ZERO studies showing pain worsening—(1) Gupta et al. 2010 (PMID:22247833, PMC3255384, oral ethanolic leaf extract reducing acetic-acid writhing and thermal pain); (2) Patil et al. 2012 (PMID:22345863, PMC3271532, acute and chronic oral methanolic leaf extract easing tail-immersion, hot-plate, and writhing pain); (3) Mani et al. 2013 (PMID:23360913, oral total alkaloidal leaf extract easing writhing, hot-plate, and formalin pain); (4) Gupta et al. 2013 (PMID:23852898, oral aqueous leaf extract naloxone-blocked analgesia); (5) Sharmin Ani et al. 2016 (PMID:27812367, PMC5080466, oral methanolic leaf extract inhibiting glutamate pain via K-ATP channels); and (6) Tembhurne & Sakarkar 2010 (PMID:21589767, PMC3093092, oral leaf extract attenuating diabetic neuropathic hyperalgesia/allodynia in rats). Zero human pain trials, raw extracts vs cooked culinary leaves, and non-PD animal models cap confidence strictly at minimal_signal.

No human Parkinson's balance trial tests cooked Murraya koenigii leaves, and preclinical dopaminergic/motor models directly conflict across leaf fractions: whereas Anjum 2025 (rotenone mice, paywalled methods) and Reddy 2020 (paraquat rats, inconsistent significance reporting) plus isolated isolongifolene (Balakrishnan 2021, PMID:33220427) reported improved beam/rotarod performance, Patil & Langade 2021 found petroleum-ether and alkaloid M. koenigii leaf fractions PROLONGED haloperidol catalepsy and REDUCED apomorphine movement (anti-dopaminergic action). Consistent with Round 1, postural instability remains open.

No human gait-kinematics trial or rodent stride-length assay tests ground Murraya koenigii leaves. Preclinical rodent and fly motor models (Shabir 2022, PMC9405140 Drosophila climbing; Anjum 2025; Patil & Langade 2021 catalepsy prolongation) conflict across extracts and do not measure stride length.
No human dysarthria or listener-rated speech intelligibility trial evaluates cooked Murraya koenigii leaves in Parkinson's disease.

No isolated clinical trial tests cooked Murraya koenigii leaves for urinary urgency or overactive bladder. Sengupta et al. 2011 (PMID:22177370, n=46 men with benign prostatic hyperplasia) conducted a double-blind double-dummy RCT comparing a BUNDLED 2-herb formulation of standardized Murraya koenigii PLUS Tribulus terrestris leaves against tamsulosin with NO placebo arm (IPSS declined 17->9 vs 14->8). Co-formulation with Tribulus terrestris, absence of placebo control, BPH obstruction versus PD neurogenic detrusor overactivity, and extract capsules vs cooked leaves prevent attributing urinary urgency relief to cooked curry leaf.

No human clinical trial, pharmacovigilance series, or Parkinson's psychosis cohort evaluates ground Murraya koenigii leaves on visual hallucinations. Ex vivo mouse brain-slice assays (Sireesha & Vidyavathi 2023) do not model visual hallucinations.

No human walking-speed trial tests ground Murraya koenigii leaves in Parkinson's disease, and preclinical dopaminergic motor models directly conflict across leaf fractions—consistent with Round 1 0027/0092/0303/0443 all kept open. While aqueous/extract studies reported improved open-field/beam locomotion in paraquat rats (Reddy 2020, inconsistent significance reporting), rotenone mice (Anjum 2025, paywalled full methods), and rotenone fruit flies (Shabir 2022, PMC9405140), Patil & Langade 2021 found petroleum-ether and alkaloid M. koenigii leaf fractions PROLONGED haloperidol catalepsy and REDUCED apomorphine-induced locomotion. Isolated minor terpene isolongifolene (Balakrishnan 2021, PMID:33220427) does not represent culinary ground leaf. Walking slowness remains open.

No human clinical trial measures apathy severity (e.g., Starkstein Apathy Scale, LARS, MDS-UPDRS 1.5) under plain dark chocolate. Historical ethnomedicinal records compiled in Dillinger 2000 (PMID:10917925) note traditional cacao preparations for apathetic or exhausted patients (customary_use, context-only), and Wolz 2012 (n=26 PD) assessed only composite motor score. Remains open.

Controlled human crossovers directly testing plain dark chocolate (Sasaki 2024 PMC10803911 n=18, Stroop attention accuracy p=0.014/0.006; Field 2011 n=30 dark vs white chocolate CRT; Sumiyoshi 2019 n=18) and cocoa flavanol beverages (Scholey 2010 n=30 RVIP; Karabay 2018 n=48 visual search; Desideri 2012 n=90 MCI & Mastroiacovo 2015 n=90 older adults TMT-A p<0.0001) provide a modest non-PD easing lean. Substantially tempered by major null trials including COSMOS-Mind (n=2,262, 3-yr cocoa extract global cognition p=0.28), FlaSeCo 2020 (n=100 plain dark chocolate TMT-A p=0.93), Altinok 2025 (n=36), Akyurek 2024 (n=48), adverse bundled DHA+dark chocolate in CANN 2023 (n=197), and absence of PD trials, capping confidence at minimal_signal.

Wolz 2012 (PMID:22584952, n=26 PD single-dose crossover of 200 g 80% dark vs white chocolate) reported a null between-treatment composite UPDRS-III contrast (-0.54 +/- 0.47, 95% CI -1.50 to 0.42, p=0.258) without separating bradykinesia subscores; NCT02275884 lacks posted results; Wolz 2009 and Schaeffer 2021 measured chocolate consumption frequency rather than motor efficacy; Al-Okbi 2025 (PMC12227552) measured rotenone-rat brain/gut biomarkers with zero motor behavioral tests; and a 2023 PD forum user noted dark chocolate and fava beans were insufficient for motor slowing. Remains open.

Fox 2019 (PMID:30912735, n=16 randomized crossover of 100 g/d 72% plain dark chocolate vs 0% white chocolate for 5 days) directly demonstrated firmer stools (BSS 3 [3-5] vs 4 [4-6], p=0.011) alongside a trend to slower colonic transit (21 vs 17 h, p=0.075), corroborated by Muller-Lissner 2005 (n=1,088 survey identifying chocolate as the top perceived constipating food, 48-64%). Fiber-enriched soluble cocoa powder drinks (Sarria 2012) and pediatric cocoa-husk fiber supplements (Castillejo 2006) ease bowel transit via added dietary fiber rather than plain solid dark chocolate (exposure_fit=unusable). Because Fox 2019 studied healthy non-constipated volunteers whose BSS remained within normal range (3 vs 4) and no PD trial exists, evidence stays at minimal_signal for worsening.

No controlled human trial or Parkinson's cohort isolates daily off time under plain dark chocolate. Wolz 2012 (PMID:22584952, n=26 PD single-dose 200 g 80% dark vs white chocolate crossover) reported a null between-treatment composite UPDRS-III contrast (-0.54 +/- 0.47, 95% CI -1.50 to 0.42, p=0.258) without isolating this symptom, NCT02275884 (1-week PD dark vs white chocolate) lacks posted results, and Al-Okbi 2025 (rotenone rat study) reported biochemical/microbiota endpoints without motor-symptom behavior. Claim remains open.

No randomized trial evaluates plain dark chocolate on Epworth Sleepiness Scale or clinical daytime somnolence. Grassi 2016 (PMID:27088635, n=32 crossover) showed flavanol-rich chocolate preserved working memory in women and improved arterial FMD/BP after one night of total sleep deprivation without reporting a daytime sleepiness severity improvement, and Wolz 2012 (n=26 PD) assessed only motor UPDRS-III. Remains open.

Direct plain dark-chocolate RCTs outside PD favor easing depressive symptoms rather than worsening: Abdoli 2024 (PMC11471752, n=60 8-wk triple-blind RCT, 78% dark vs milk chocolate MD -2.3, 95% CI -3.9 to -0.8, p=0.003), Shin 2022 (PMID:34530112, n=48 3-wk RCT, 85% dark chocolate reduced PANAS negative affect p<0.05), and Sathyapalan 2010 (PMC3001690, n=10 CFS DB crossover, improved HADS), backed by NHANES (Jackson 2019, n=13,626) and Fusar-Poli 2022 meta-analysis (Hedges' g -0.42, 95% CI -0.67 to -0.17). Tempered by FlaSeCo 2020 (n=100 older adults, null depression contrast between high/low flavanol dark chocolate), mixed PD community experiences (Parkinson's UK 2009/2020/2023), and zero PD RCTs, capping confidence at minimal_signal.

No controlled clinical study or cohort evaluates plain dark chocolate on dream enactment behavior (DEB) frequency. Vorona & Ware 2002 (PMID:14592201, n=1 clinical case report, cited in Jun 2022 PMC9519124) reported possible RBD exacerbation following unspecified chocolate ingestion; a single uncontrolled case without specified dark-chocolate preparation, dose, or PD diagnosis is insufficient to sign a directional tier, leaving the claim open.

No controlled human trial or Parkinson's cohort isolates drooling severity under plain dark chocolate. Three independent rodent depression models using dried Ajwa or P. dactylifera fruit pulp extracts—Asdaq et al. 2025 (PMID:41224947, CMS mice sucrose preference/TST p<0.001), Shivanandappa et al. 2023 (PMID:37445591, PMC10341400, LPS sickness rats FST/TST p<0.01-0.001), and Youssef et al. 2022 (PMID:35348229, CUMS rats FST/grooming)—all showed statistically significant antidepressant-like reductions in behavioral despair. Cardiometabolic reviews (Jim et al. 2025 PMID:41464915) identify zero trials measuring supine-to-standing orthostatic blood pressure or postprandial orthostatic lightheadedness in Parkinson disease.

Evidence remains open for dried dates affecting postural instability severity in Parkinson disease. Zero human clinical trials have tested whole dried Phoenix dactylifera fruit on Parkinson motor signs. Preclinical rodent motor observations are indirect, non-PD, and directionally mixed: Subash et al. 2015 (PMID:26167001) observed improved rotarod coordination in transgenic Alzheimer Tg2576 mice fed 2-4% Oman date chow, and Zangiabadi et al. 2011 (PMID:22191015, PMC3236446) preserved peripheral sciatic nerve conduction and exploratory activity in diabetic neuropathy rats, whereas Sheikh et al. 2016 (PMID:27746708, PMC5040737) reported reduced spontaneous locomotor activity from ethanol date-fruit extracts in mice. Ongoing registered PD fiber-bar protocols (NCT07127120, NCT07914387) bundle date paste with prebiotic fibers without published motor results, and a retracted date-seed rat paper (PMID:36654869) is strictly excluded.

One human randomized clinical trial specifically testing oral Anethum graveolens seed (10 g boiled in 100 mL water, filtered) vs IV oxytocin during active childbirth (PMID:31705450, n=100) found fewer women in the severe/almost-severe STAI trait (0% vs 8%/14%, p=0.050) and state (0% vs 14%, p=0.041) anxiety categories 6 hours postpartum. Major transfer gaps — boiled infusion vs frozen toasted seed, open-label active oxytocin comparator rather than placebo, obstetric labor context (with shorter labor confounding anxiety), categorical reporting, and no Parkinson's trial — limit the tier to minimal_signal; perinatal mouse maze data (Maodaa 2025) remain contextual due to unspecified plant organ and statistical anomalies.

No human clinical or animal study evaluates ground dill seed on apathy severity in Parkinson's disease; human A. graveolens RCTs have examined dysmenorrhea, labor, and cardiometabolic lipids/insulin (PMID:33624557) without apathy endpoints, keeping the claim open.

No human clinical trial tests toasted dill seed on attention impairment in Parkinson's disease; Mesripour et al. (2016, PMID:27168754) used intraperitoneal Anethum essence (non-oral, unspecified plant part) on scopolamine novel-object recognition in mice, and Sharma et al. (2024, LOCAL:Sharma2024) tested dill seed solvent extracts only in H2O2-stressed SH-SY5Y cells and acellular AChE assays, leaving the claim open.

No human PD or mammalian PD-model study tests ground dill seed on bradykinesia severity; only SH-SY5Y H2O2 neuroprotection by dill seed extracts (LOCAL:Sharma2024), injected mouse locomotion assays (LOCAL:RaczKotilla1996), and isolated (S)-(+)-carvone ambulation suppression (PMID:17299731) exist, keeping the claim open.

No human clinical trial or mammalian constipation model isolates Anethum graveolens seed on constipation severity; the T2DM colonic-motility trial (PMC7275438, Haidari 2020, n=42) explicitly milled dried dill LEAVES rather than seeds and reported only a within-group chi-square (p=0.010) on a pooled colonic-motility category without a between-group test, the IBS RCT bundled three herbal oils (PMID:32565786), ex vivo rat ileum work tested aerial parts (LOCAL:Gocmanac2015), and mouse seed extract testing evaluated gastric ulcers rather than bowel transit (PMID:12493079), keeping the claim open.

No clinical or animal levodopa-fluctuation study tests ground dill seed on daily off time; only cellular dill seed antioxidant assays (LOCAL:Sharma2024) and cardiometabolic RCTs (PMID:33624557) exist, keeping the claim open.

No human clinical trial evaluates toasted dill seed on daytime sleepiness severity; isolated (S)-(+)-carvone (dill seed constituent) increased sedation and reduced ambulation in non-PD mice (PMID:17299731) and injected dill extracts reduced mouse locomotion (LOCAL:RaczKotilla1996), neither of which tests oral toasted dill seed or human ESS sleepiness, keeping the claim open.

Two independent human clinical trials specifically testing oral Anethum graveolens seed on visceral menstrual pain point toward easing rather than worsening: a double-blind RCT of ground dill seed powder capsules (2,000 mg/d x 5 d for 2 cycles, n=70 analyzed, PMID:25097605/PMC4115348) reduced primary dysmenorrhea VAS pain vs baseline (p<0.0001), matched mefenamic acid (MD 0.13, 95% CI -1.01 to 1.27), and outperformed placebo in Cochrane's extraction (MD -1.15 VAS points, 95% CI -2.22 to -0.08, n=46, PMID:27000311), corroborated by a 3-arm comparative trial where 3 g/d dill seeds eased dysmenorrhea pain (PMID:31383440, n=31). Small samples, Cochrane low/very low quality, and dysmenorrhea-to-PD pain transfer gaps cap the tier at minimal_signal (easing -> Maybe False against the worsening hypothesis).
